Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that on February 2 I informed hon. members that a sale of 40 million bushels of wheat and barley, valued at approximately $60 million, had been contracted between the Canadian wheat board and the China Resources Company.
I now inform the house that there was an additional sale to China of 2.2 million bushels of wheat, valued at $3.7 million, for shipment during March to May, 1961. Those connected with shipping grain through the west coast ports have made a fine effort to meet these commitments. As a result, the grain sold to China for delivery between March and August is being loaded ahead of schedule.
Simultaneously with the fulfilling of the first order there have been discussions and finally negotiations between the Canadian wheat board and the China Resources Company concerning further amounts of grain that could be made available. Because of the quantities of grain involved and other factors, the Canadian government felt there should be an over-all agreement to facilitate orderly marketing.
I am now pleased to report that a long term agreement has been signed. This long term agreement covers the period June 1,
1961	to December, 1963. Under this agreement we have committed ourselves to provide up to six million tons of barley, wheat and flour. Of this amount approximately one million tons will be barley. To put this into approximate bushels and value, it would provisionally be 186.7 million bushels of wheat and 46.7 million bushels of barley, worth approximately $362 million.
If one adds the previous order for 28 million bushels of wheat and 12 million bushels of barley, valued at $60 million, then the total transaction that could provisionally be expected for the three calendar years 1961,
1962	and 1963 will be 217 million bushels of wheat and 58.8 million bushels of barley, with a total approximate value of $425.6 million.
I mentioned earlier that the first order of 40 million bushels was being moved satisfactorily. As an extension to the order now being filled, a contract to provide additional grain from June 1 to November 30 of this year has been signed. It is the first contract under the long term agreement. The amounts are 750,000 long tons of wheat, 360,000 long tons of barley and 32,500 tons of flour, to be shipped mainly from west coast ports. The equivalent in bushels is 28 million bushels of wheat, 17 million bushels of barley and 1.5 million bushels of flour. The estimated value of this order is $66 million. The terms of payment under the long term agreement are 25 per cent cash and the balance in 270 days.
Hon. members will appreciate that it is beyond the resources of the Canadian wheat board to extend credit facilities for the quantities involved in these transactions. Accordingly the government, reflecting its intensive efforts to sell grain in volume to new markets, is prepared to guarantee to a maximum of $50 million the credit necessary for the Canadian wheat board to conclude these transactions on a short term credit basis. I have made it clear that there is a long term agreement. Under that agreement one contract has been signed. Each future contract will be negotiated in respect to price and quantity.
A sale of this order will spread substantial benefits through the Canadian economy. Not only will it provide a welcome increase in western farm incomes, but this in turn will release new purchasing power for the goods and services required by farmers from the business community at large. Additionally the sale will generate increased employment for country and terminal elevator operators, railway and dock workers, and others engaged in the domestic handling and export movement of grain and flour. It is apparent that new grain sales of this magnitude will add significantly to Canada's total earnings from exports. Business activity in general will therefore be stimulated to a marked extent by the conclusion of this new sales contract with China.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposilion):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We on this side welcome the minister back from his trip across the Pacific to Hong Kong, where he has been successful in negotiating a long term agreement with

Sale of Grain to China the communist government of China and a considerable sale of wheat, barley and flour for the current year 1961.
So far as the long term agreement is concerned we can only hope on this side that an agreement of this kind negotiated with a government of this type will work out satisfactorily for our own country. There is, of course, an element of insecurity in an agreement negotiated with this kind of government, because political considerations often intervene between the purchaser and the seller. It is perhaps somewhat ironic that famine in red China, a country with which we have no diplomatic relations, has meant this large sale of grain which we welcome. We welcome also the reduction in our surplus together with the increased activity that the sale will provide.
But, of course, this is not normal trade. This is a windfall. Two factors make this sale even more unusual. One is that credit terms are now being given to the communist government of China, as mentioned by the minister. We sell wheat to our friends for cash. We sell it now to a government which we do not recognize diplomatically, for credit. Also the minister is reported as stating at a press conference in Vancouver that we shall accept pounds sterling for this sale, pounds acquired by communist China through the sale of rice to sterling countries.
It is clear, of course, that the United States is not a competitor for this trade, because United States trade with China in all commodities is now illegal. While that is not a reason why we should not develop our own trade with China in commodities which are not on the strategic list, a position we have taken on this side for some years, this deal, however, undoubtedly will mean that the United States may not feel itself under the same obligations as it was previously in co-operating with us in the sale of agricultural products abroad.
Considerations governing this arrangement show that in government thinking there is a distinction to be observed-and this applies also to South African developments-between political ideology and commercial advantage, and that political ideology does not prevent a commercial embrace.
Mr. Speaker, if my memory serves me correctly the former Liberal government sold wheat to Poland on long term credit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We recognized Poland diplomatically.

Mr. Speaker, I am perhaps out of my element in commenting on this subject, but if the hon. member for Assiniboia
[Mr. Pearson.)

were here he would say that we welcome this announcement. We are glad the minister has been able to make this contract for the sale of this wheat, but with over 500 million bushels of surplus grain on the prairies and with an annual production of grain of approximately 500 million bushels, the minister must continue actively searching for markets which will bring even greater results if we are going to meet the needs and the expectations of the producers of grain in western Canada, for whom I speak today.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture arising out of his interesting statement this morning. Did the minister indicate in Vancouver yesterday that payment for some of the grain to be sold to communist China would be in pounds sterling; and if so, what proportion of the payment would likely be made in pounds sterling?
Second, in his statement I think the minister said that the shipments would be made mainly from west coast ports. Have any deliveries so far, under the agreement which commenced in February, been made out of eastern Canadian ports, and does the minister contemplate that some deliveries will be necessary from other than west coast ports during the 1960-61 shipping season?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, dealing with the portion of the question concerning shipping, all the first order has been shipped through the four west coast ports. If the additional orders starting in June overlap the previous orders it will be necessary to ship a portion of them, about 300,000 tons out of the 1.2 million tons, out of the St. Lawrence ports.
With regard to the part of the question dealing with sterling, as I understand it all the payments will be made in sterling.

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture and ask whether he is aware of the fact that the port of Prince Rupert is 500 miles nearer to the Orient than Vancouver, and every opportunity should be taken to use the grain terminal facilities there.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member had been following the announcements which I have been making these last three or four months he would understand that the port of Prince Rupert has never been so busy, and that situation will probably continue for some time to come.
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Does the minister not realize that I only want to see it busier?

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, in accordance with notice which I gave orally last week I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa West:
That the annual report of the governor of the Bank of Canada to the Minister of Finance and statement of accounts for the year 1960 be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce for study.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Undoubtedly the hon. member has considered whether this motion can properly be made, and if he can indicate any precedent for a motion of this kind I would appreciate him doing so now.

Mr. Speaker, last week this matter was discussed. The report of the discussion will be found at pages 4043 and 4044 of Hansard of April 27, 1961. The presiding officer of the chamber at that time took the position that under citation 186 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, there would be difficulty in a private member of this house giving oral notice in respect of a motion of this sort. It was pointed out that under that citation certain exceptions were provided in respect of routine proceedings. It was argued per contra that this involved proceedings affecting the maintenance of the authority of this house.
Some discussion took place between the presiding officer at that time and the member for Essex East, later participated in by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. The remarks of the Deputy Speaker, to be found at page 4044 of Hansard of April 27, 1961, I believe support and warrant the initiative taken by me this morning. He observed, as reported in the right hand column at the bottom of the page as follows:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the comments of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate have clarified the point. As he says, if the notice given by the hon. member for Essex East is not intended to have this question stand on the order paper, there is no problem-
Then later on at page 4045, in the left hand column, about a quarter way down the page, he says:
I do not think that is necessary because the question seems very clear and, as I said, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has removed any doubt I might have had.
Inquiries of the Ministry
I believe I should be frank in this matter, Mr. Speaker. At the time I myself had understood that the Deputy Speaker had taken a position against the submission I had made, but on a careful perusal of Hansard, as I am now indicating by some excerpts, it is clear I think that the Deputy Speaker did in fact concur in the clarification so ably provided by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
On the merits, Mr. Speaker, the submission briefly is that, under the Bank of Canada Act, the governor of the Bank of Canada is responsible only to parliament, according to the Minister of Finance. By way of parenthesis I say, of course, that exception is taken to that interpretation of the governor's constitutional and legal responsibilities. Nevertheless, in part, that is the legal position; the governor is responsible to parliament with respect to monetary policy. His report is in the hands of the government and has been made available to members of this house, but no opportunity exists for an examination of its contents, based upon interrogation of the governor or otherwise. It would seem to me incomprehensible that the governor of the Bank of Canada, who is responsible to parliament, should not be available for questioning by parliament. This brings the matter within the bounds of what is a routine proceeding, and is covered by the explanation of citation 186 and clarified by the ruling which Mr. Deputy Speaker gave on April 27.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I submit that this written motion of mine, oral notice of which was given last week, is in order. It is the only procedure available to this house in view of the government's reluctance to have the report of the Bank of Canada placed before a committee of the house for consideration. It would render completely ridiculous the legal responsibility of the Bank of Canada to parliament if parliament was not given the opportunity in the face of the government's refusal and reluctance, to examine the report of the Bank of Canada. It would mean that the governor was not responsible to parliament in fact but was responsible only to the government, a contention that is denied by the government.
For these reasons I submit that this motion is in order and that the house ought to be given a chance of passing judgment on the merits.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has perhaps served his purpose in trying to discuss the issue that he would like to raise today under the disguise of a point of order. The point of order, Mr. Speaker, is quite clear and the Deputy Speaker of the house,

Inquiries of the Ministry who was in the chair on April 27, has dealt with the matter completely and succinctly. When the hon. member for Essex East sought to raise the matter and to purport to give an oral notice, the Deputy Speaker, as appears at page 4043 of Hansard, quoted citation 186 from Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, as follows:
Oral notices for future proceedings do not exist in the Canadian House of Commons.
As the discussion proceeded I read the remainder of the citation, which simply confirms the ruling that was made by the Deputy Speaker at that time; because by no stretch of the imagination could what the hon. member for Essex East is attempting to do here now be possibly justified in view of the terms of citation 186. What was attempted by him at that time was a complete nullity, and what is attempted by him here today is, under the rules of the house, a complete nullity. He is seeking to make new rules to fit the occasion, Mr. Speaker, and those rules are not to be made in quite this way. The only way such a private member's motion could proceed would be by unanimous consent, and that unanimous consent is not given.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I could say a word before you make your decision on this point. In the first place, sir, it seems to me, however much respect we may pay to citations from Beauchesne, that when one examines the standing orders of the house one will find there is no prohibition against a private member getting up and moving a motion having to do with routine proceedings. In fact that is done practically every day in the house, as Your Honour well knows and as is pointed out in the citation referred to by the hon. member for Essex East.
Only yesterday there was at least one motion, if not two, for concurrence in the report of a committee moved by the person who is chairman of that committee but who in the house is merely a private member. Moreover, motions are frequently made to change the composition of a committee and, in fact, one was made yesterday by the hon. member for Elgin.
There have been occasions-I remember well when the question first arose in recent times-when there has not been concurrence in these motions being moved immediately; and the question of notice, which was never published anywhere, was settled, I think, by Mr. Speaker Macdonald by a suggestion that they might be printed in routine proceedings, but there is no such requirement in the rules.
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) .1
Fundamentally, the point I wish to make is a very simple one. It is a recognized principle of our constitution, one particularly dear to those of us on this side of the house, that we have responsible government in this country and that the executive is responsible to the house. It seems to me, in default of any specific prohibition in the rules, that it must be assumed that there is a procedure, a method, by which that responsibility can be exercised, and that it certainly would be a denial of the rights of hon. members to deny them the possibility of testing the views of the house with respect to whether any report should be referred to a committee.
The government should not have control of that. That should be in the control of the house, even where the report in question is a report made to the house by a government department. But the situation, of course, is tremendously aggravated in this particular instance by the view taken by the government that it has no responsibility and that there is a direct responsibility to this chamber.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member in that line of argument is perhaps dealing more with the merits of the motion than with the point of order.

It was only the aspect of order with which I was seeking to deal. If this house is to exercise that responsibility which we have under the constitution, it is important that members of the opposition should be able to make the necessary routine motions in an effective way when the government does not do it, and this is particularly important where it is argued that there is no direct responsibility to the government.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will say no more than this. In the years I have been here and when hon. gentlemen opposite were in the government, at no time was it ever permissible for a private member to move the type of motion that has been moved today. When the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate talks about those on the other side now believing in responsible government, I am glad they have at last achieved a belief in something they so continually disregarded when they sat over here. I simply point out, and it is interesting to note this, that after all their examination, which must have been meticulously careful, they were unable to find one example to support them in their contention.
Where is your championing of the rights of parliament now?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the practice, procedure and interpretation of the rules are reasonably clear. There are two matters involved in the motion submitted by the hon. member for Essex East. The first is the question of whether oral notice of motion can be given, and that was discussed the other day. I think our standing orders and practice are clear, and I refer the house to standing order 41 which reads as follows:
Forty-eight hours' notice shall be given of a motion for leave to present a bill, resolution or address .. . Such notice shall be laid on the table before six o'clock p.m., and be printed in the Votes and Proceedings of that day.
Then I refer to Bourinot, fourth edition, page 295, where he says:
In the House of Commons, when a member has prepared his notice of motion in writing, he hands it to the Clerk ...
Further on the same point, citation 186 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, reads in part as follows:
Oral notices for future proceedings do not exist in the Canadian House of Commons.
I think it is fair to conclude that this is a well established practice in our house. Whenever a notice is required it has to be in writing. In standing order 42 it is provided that in certain cases notice may be waived by the house, but that involves unanimous consent, and it is not the case which falls for decision.
The other point is whether notice of motion of this kind can be brought on routine proceedings and, if so, by a private member. The hon. member for Essex East has failed to produce any precedent for the rather unusual course which he suggests. Motions made during routine proceedings include motions relating to the business of the house, according to Bourinot, fourth edition, page 219, footnote (s). On the same subject Beauchesne says in citation 85 of his fourth edition:
The motions allowed on routine proceedings are motions relating to the business of the house and for the discussion of reports from committees.
Standing order 32 of our rules, subparagraph (1) (m), gives us a general idea of the kind of motions which can be made during routine proceedings, and I refer hon. members to subparagraph (m) of this order which is the order relating to debatable motions. Subparagraph (m) says that the following motions are debatable:
(m) such other motion, made upon routine proceedings, as may be required for the observance of the proprieties of the house, the maintenance of its authority, the appointment or conduct of its officers, the management of its business, the arrangements of its proceedings, the correctness of its records, the fixing of its sitting days or the times of its meeting or adjournment.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Assuming only for the purpose of argument that this motion does relate to the business of the house, which I shall deal with later, the further question remains whether it could be moved by a private member. It is well established and certainly has been the normal practice that the responsibility for the business of the house and for initiating motions with respect to the business of the house rests with the house leader. Motions which might come under that section are motions relating to the time of sitting as well as the business of the house, approving appointments, transfers, dismissal or retirement by the civil service commission of certain officers of the house, expressing sympathy for the death of some prominent person, or acknowledging any gift made to the house, or accepting or making any invitation, or making an unimportant correction in the debates, Votes and Proceeding and Journals of the house, or for the election of the chairman of committees of the whole house or for the appointment of the special selection committee. Questions of privilege, when raised under routine proceedings, also come within that category.
At any rate, that is the type of motion admitted. I think it might be worth while to put Bourinot's further views on record. In his fourth edition, at page 301, he says:
Motions applying to the business or arrangements of the house are called, in the ordinary daily routine, after the presentation of committee reports and before the introduction of bills. As a rule these motions require notice, but some are of such a purely formal nature that by general consent notice is not insisted upon.
Also Beauchesne in citation 87:
It is a fundamental rule that with the exception of certain matters dealt with under routine proceedings, no question can be considered by the house unless it has been previously appointed either by a notice or a regular order of the house.
Then citation 88 (2):
All motions referring to the business of the house should be introduced by the leader of the house.
I think it is reasonably clear that the business of the house is normally introduced by a motion of the house leader, and it is also reasonably clear what type of transaction is included in the business of the house.
There are some instances of the kind of motion which the hon. member for Essex East has in mind and of how they have been dealt with. I have just picked out two for the information of the house. They are quite recent. They are instances from last year. I have here the Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day for Monday, March 7, 1960. At page 2 under the heading of "Daily Routine of Business" there are listed the following:
Introduction of bills; first reading of Senate public bills; Government notices of motions.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The government notice of motion for that day was one standing in the name of the Minister of Finance, as follows:
That the public accounts I and II, and the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ... he referred to the standing committee on public accounts.
That is a motion of this type and it was dealt with on the motion of the Minister of Finance, under government notices of motion. It was then, of course, transferred to and dealt with as a government order in due course. The same thing is found on Friday, March 11, 1960, where under the name of the Prime Minister, under the heading of government notices of motions, stands the following motion:
That the report of the Canada Council for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1959.... be referred to the standing committee on public accounts-
And so on. This proposed motion is about a report of the Bank of Canada or deals with a report of the Bank of Canada, which, as the hon. member says, is required to be made to parliament under the Bank of Canada Act, and is of the same order and character as the two reports or documents referred to committees by the government under notices of motion, as I have indicated, and dealt with subsequently under government orders.
The hon. member raises the question of whether a private member can do the same thing. I think it is clear that a private member can do so if he can use the notice of motion procedure which is open to private members under our rules. But, of course, that procedure would involve the giving of written notice of 48 hours. The notice of motion would then appear on the order paper at a place where, at this stage of the session, it could not be dealt with.
The hon. member's complaint, I take it, is that because this motion cannot be dealt with in the way that is normally open to a private member, therefore there must be some way of dealing with it under our rules. I think that is the fallacy of the argument. Our rules speak for themselves and our practice has been settled. We must interpret them as they are. If they are defective in not giving a private member of the house an opportunity to make a motion which he feels he should make, or to take a procedure which he feels he should take, the remedy is to amend the rules, not to depart from the practice which has been well established.
I therefore think I must follow what appears to me to be the logical course and indicate to the hon. member that I do not think he, as a private member, without notice, can make the motion which he proposes to make except with the unanimous consent of the house. I think that covers most


of the points that have been raised and is my best judgment of our practice as it applies to the hon. member's motion.

Mr. Speaker, I rise not to take issue with your ruling, but first of all to thank you for the great care you have obviously taken in trying to protect the rights of the private members of this house.
You have said that in your judgment there is no procedure open to a private member to make the kind of motion which I submitted a few moments ago. However, in the course of your remarks you made the observation that it would be permissible to seek to raise the matter in another by way of a question of privilege. Whether Your Honour had made this observation or not, in my effort to exhaust the possibilities open to us I was about to raise-in the light of your ruling, not in contempt of it-a question of privilege.
My question of privilege is one that affects me as a private member of this house, and indeed it is a question that affects the privileges of all members of this house. The question of privilege is that we are not given the opportunity which I believe duty demands of us in the examination of a document which is now in the possession of the house and which in my judgment-

Order. Before the hon. member proceeds may I make this observation. If his question of privilege is what he appears to indicate now, I am afraid he is not warranted in trying to make a matter of privilege out of a point of order. The rules of the house are set by the house itself. It is not a breach of the privileges of the house to observe its own rules.
I think I perhaps omitted one point which the hon. member made and which he asserts as a privilege, namely that there is no opportunity for him as a private member to deal with this situation which he feels should be dealt with. I do not accept that assertion. There are other opportunities in the procedure of the house to raise the question of the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada. The only thing that I am proscribing this morning is a motion by a private member, made without notice upon routine proceedings to refer that report to a committee. Other opportunities and courses may be open to the hon. member. I am sorry that I cannot accept his question of privilege. I therefore consider the matter closed.

May I say that I have a motion based on the question of

privilege, which I have not completed and which is incorporated in the following motion:
Whereas the bank-

The motion is as follows:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but he is really presenting an argument here under the guise of a motion of privilege. I am afraid he has taken the wrong course. speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I certainly like to hear the hon. gentleman talk, but I think after you make a ruling that ruling should be observed. I thought a ruling had definitely been made. The hon. gentleman persists in this course, which he must know -I say he must know-is contrary to the rules of the house, and I ask Your Honour to proceed accordingly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The right hon. Prime Minister is quite right in saying that when I have come to a conclusion, as I have both on the point of order and on the question of privilege, the matter is then disposed of. The other course open to the hon. member is to appeal the ruling that has been given.
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to appeal your ruling-
Order.
Then sit down.

-but I do propose to say to the Prime Minister that I am not yet of the disposition to accept lectures from him.
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Prime Minister is within his rights, as the hon. member recognizes, in drawing attention to the fact that a ruling has been made. The question of privilege has been disposed of and the matter is closed.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-86, an act to amend the Fisheries Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of Bill No. C-86 I should like at the outset to point out that, with the exception of some minor amendments, the last one of which was made in 1949, there have been no major changes in the act since 1932.
The Fisheries Act is the basic statute under which the fisheries of Canada are administered. In the last three decades many new problems in the administration of fisheries have arisen, problems created by the variety of species involved and the geographical distribution of the fisheries, as well as problems arising out of federal-provincial responsibilities for the development of the fisheries and the international character of the sea fisheries adjacent to our extensive coast lines.
During the same period much progress has been made in biological and technological research and the development of new fishing vessels and fishing gear. It has therefore become necessary to amend the basic act under which the fisheries of Canada are administered, so as to bring it into line with present day requirements and practice.
One of the difficult problems arising out of the existing provisions of the act relates to the arbitrary exclusion of Canadian trawlers from the 12 mile coastal zone in the Atlantic coast provinces. This exclusion of fishing vessels using an otter trawl has been part of the law of Canada for more than half a century. During that time fishing by draggers has increased to the point where we now have on the Atlantic coast about 281 small draggers operated by Canadian fishermen and about 75 large draggers, sometimes called trawlers. This method of fishing now accounts for about 40 per cent of our total production of groundfish on the Atlantic seaboard of Canada.
Following world war II the advent in increased numbers of foreign fishing vessels to areas along our coasts, particularly off the coast of Nova Scotia, has created the anomalous situation where foreign trawlers in certain areas fish up to the three mile international limit, whereas Canadian trawlers are not permitted to come closer than 12 miles in the same areas. This 12 mile restriction

applies only in the maritime provinces. It does not apply to Newfoundland where, by virtue of arrangements made at the time of the union of Newfoundland with Canada, the Fisheries Act was amended so as to permit Canadian trawlers to fish up to the three mile limit. It does not apply on the west coast of Canada.
The minister is given authority under the act to exempt small draggers from the 12 mile prohibition. This exemption has been accorded to small draggers 65 feet in length and under for a number of years, and they may fish up to the shore line in all areas with the exception of those where, by regulation, zones have been established within which their operation is banned, subject to the restriction that they will not interfere with the other methods of fishing. The minister has, however, no authority under the existing section of the act to except larger draggers from the 12 mile prohibition.
An amendment to section 55 of the act is therefore proposed which would give the minister the same authority with respect to the larger draggers that he now has with respect to small draggers, but only in areas designated by him between three and 12 miles from the coast of the Atlantic sea coast provinces excepting Newfoundland, where, as I have pointed out, the 12 mile restriction has been reduced to three miles by an amendment in 1949. The proposed amendment would enable the minister to establish zones where fishing by larger draggers would be permitted. The establishment of such zones would be undertaken with due regard to the interests of local fishermen.
Another problem for which a solution must be found, by providing a more flexible regulatory system, refers to the necessity for rapid closures or extensions of fishing times, particularly in the case of the anadromous species such as salmon, the runs of which to spawning streams and lakes are closely watched on a day to day basis and where a set fishing season may have to be closed or extended on short notice. In such instances it becomes virtually impossible to enforce proper conservation measures without giving regional and provincial officials the necessary authority for that purpose. The proposed amendments would empower the governor in council to prescribe this required authority.
Another subject requiring attention relates to the removal of any doubts that the act and any regulations enacted under it apply to Canadian nationals and fishing vessels not only in the territorial waters but also on the high seas. It is trite to say that fish take no cognizance of arbitrary boundary lines, and it is not possible to provide adequate con-90205-6-266J
Fisheries Act
servation measures in respect to any species that migrate freely in and out of the territorial waters unless fishing activities can be regulated inside as well as beyond the territorial waters either unilaterally, in cases where only Canadian fishermen are involved, or by international agreement where fishermen of other states fish in the high seas for the same stock of fish. One of the proposed amendments to the act would clarify the scope of the application of the act.
In recent times problems of pollution of waters frequented by fish have become accentuated. The sections of the act dealing with pollution need to be strengthened in order to cope effectively with these problems. The proposed amendment would increase the penalties and make provision for giving notice to the public by the governor in council of any substance which may from time to time be found harmful to fish life.
Although in certain respects the powers of regulating under the act are inadequate for present day requirements, in other respects some of the powers contained in the act relating to enforcement of the act go beyond present day requirements. I refer to the judicial powers of fishery officers who are, by virtue of the act, justices of the peace with power to convict on view and to confiscate valuable equipment on view. While these powers may have served a useful purpose many years ago because of the lack of properly constituted courts of criminal jurisdiction in remote and isolated areas, there is little justification today for an officer of the executive branch of government to exercise judicial functions. In fact, by administrative control, these powers were seldom used in recent years.
The act is being accordingly amended to relieve fishery officers of the responsibility of exercising any judicial functions, and to place it in the hands of the courts where it more properly belongs. The enforcement sections have accordingly been rewritten in some detail.
There are other minor amendments proposed in the way of clarification, but they are very minor. Those are the main amendments to which I wish to refer. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have nothing more to say at this juncture.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to-

Fisheries Act

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member must speak from his own seat in accordance with the rules, which require him to rise in his own place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has.

I hear the Minister of Justice say "It has". I welcome that remark, as I welcome this particular bill because the minister and the house know that on March 22,

I think it was, I introduced a bill which was designed to achieve the second principle I have just mentioned, namely to revise the Fisheries Act and bring it into conformity with the bill of rights.
As I look through the bill I am very pleased to note that the sections which I had in mind and which I outlined in the explanation I gave to the house on that occasion, namely sections 19(1), 35, 51(lb), 64 and 75 have all been taken care of in this bill which we are now discussing.
This morning I was interested in the question asked of the Minister of Justice by the hon. member for Skeena about the reports that the minister is obliged to make, in accordance with standing order 40, on bills which are introduced in the house. If I understood the minister aright he indicated that he had done his duty in this regard. I take it that should mean that the report he made on this legislation should be available. Yesterday I asked the Clerk if he could let me see the reports, and he replied that they were not available at that time.
I am still not sure, in spite of what the minister said, that this bill entirely conforms with the bill of rights. I notice that it still retains one practice which I regarded as inimical to individual rights and to which I am personally opposed. The practice to which I refer is that of seizure and forfeiture of ships and property. I cannot bring myself to believe that offences committed under the Fisheries Act should be treated differently from offences committed under any other act of parliament. Under most acts of parliament which prescribe penalties for offences, the penalties consist mainly of fines and imprisonment. I think that is fair and just because we prescribe exactly the same treatment for every offender under exactly the same circumstances. But when we introduce this practice of seizing property and causing the offender to forfeit the property we are departing from the principle of equity, of fitting the punishment to the crime and of treating every offender in the same way. In many instances, and particularly in my own riding, the property is the means of a person's livelihood. Certainly under the bill of rights a person has a right to live. I think that is the most fundamental right any human being has and one that we will maintain at all costs. When you deprive a person of his livelihood, or of his means of livelihood, you deprive him of his life in theory and in some instances in fact.
He can get another job.

It is not a case of getting another job. The merits of the case depend upon the circumstances which surround it. Even though a person may not be deprived of

his livelihood there is still an inequity which is foreign to my concept of justice, because the property which might be forfeited by one person will have no relationship to the property which might be forfeit by another offender under exactly the same circumstances.
I hoped the report of the Minister of Justice would have something to say on this matter. It was for that reason I was so interested in getting the minister's report before introducing amendments which, under other circumstances, I hoped would have been made to my own bill as it passed through the house.
We readily admit that some steps must be taken to prevent unfair or undue violations of our fisheries rights, and to protect and conserve our fisheries resources. However, when an offender has only one boat and you take that away from him, you place him in a very different position from that of a big operator who may have a number of boats so that the loss of one particular boat does not affect his livelihood to any appreciable extent. The same principle is true in respect of fishing gear and nets.
This is particularly appropriate to my own constituency, where approximately 90 per cent of the fishermen are engaged in the shore fishery, either by hook and line or by net. The boats they have are small, under 40 feet in length, and if nets are used they are vital to the way these fishermen prosecute the fishery. Perhaps some fisherman may have three or four nets, but even if only one of these is confiscated that man's means of livelihood is certainly imperilled.
I regard the retention of the right to seize and cause an offender to forfeit his property as a sort of hangover from the middle ages, and something which certainly-
A Liberal government.

I am not interested in who put it there or who left it there. I am only interested in removing what I regard as an injustice, not only an injustice but an inequity. Certainly if the bill of rights has done any one thing above another it has been to focus our attention on our rights. We are now more concerned about them. After all, it was this government that took great pride in producing this bill of rights. A lot of fanfare was made about it. We had every right to expect that if things were going to be corrected, then they would be corrected in the legislation introduced by this government. I am personally surprised that the Minister of Justice would put his stamp of approval on this kind of practice.
The minister referred to another amendment which I believe will receive general
Fisheries Act
acclaim. If there was any one thing that infringed a person's rights it was the power of the fisheries officer to act as judge, jury and lord high executioner, all in one. We are glad to see that the power which made a fisheries officer a justice of the peace has now been removed. I think everyone will rejoice at that development. Under the old act, Mr. Speaker, a fisheries officer did not need to have evidence that there had been an offence. All he needed was a suspicion or a thought in his mind, and he could proceed to confiscate a fisherman's property.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That was Liberal legislation.

I am not interested in whose legislation it was. My hon. friend is not making any contribution to the debate by sitting in his seat and making these irrelevant remarks. If he wants to get up and join in the debate he will have plenty of time later on.
I was about to say, Mr. Speaker, that within the last two weeks I have had a case brought to my attention which was prosecuted under this old act that is still in force and will remain in force until this bill is passed and receives royal assent. I received a letter from a fisherman who had set out nets to catch bait for his lobster traps. Unless he can get this bait he cannot engage in the lobster fisheries. My hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Browne), will perhaps be surprised to learn that the gentleman was one of his constituents.
It sounds familiar.

Yes. This person set nets in Placentia gut, where he claims he has a right to set them. He claims he was not infringing any boundary and, in any case, there were no marks on either side of the bank to indicate where the boundaries were. He set those nets in what he claims were legal waters. However, the fisheries officer came along and confiscated them. Now the fisherman is left without any means of acquiring bait and no means of prosecuting his livelihood.
I have written a letter to the minister about this. I know he has not had time to receive it because I did not get it typed soon enough. The letter is in the mail, and I hope the minister will take prompt action to have the fisheries officer restore these nets to the owner, because it is a very serious matter to him. He told me in his letter that he was heartbroken. He is a poor man and now he has no chance at all to earn his livelihood.
These things are very serious. When an act like that can be carried out on the initiative of one person, without evidence being

Fisheries Act
required, I think that is something that should never have been permitted in the first place, and I am glad to see the power to do so is being removed under this bill. I hope the minister will not wait until this legislation receives royal assent before he takes action to have the spirit of this legislation and the spirit of the bill of rights enforced in this particular case.
The bill itself empowers the government to make regulations for the proper management and control of sea coast and inland fisheries. It is a great disappointment to me to have to point out to the minister that this bill will not take care of the most serious hazards to our Newfoundland fisheries. In my own particular riding, and this is true in practically every coastal riding of the province, the fishing grounds are located outside the three mile limit, from three miles to 12 miles offshore. Any bill which confines the authority of the government to within three miles of land is not going to deal with the most serious problem we have to face in my province.
The greatest threat to the Newfoundland fisheries, particularly in my own riding, comes from foreign draggers. Last winter the foreign draggers were particularly active. On one occasion for at least two weeks they prevented the fishermen in my riding from prosecuting the fishery at all. They could not prosecute the fishery because, as I said earlier, these fishermen use very small boats about 40 feet in length or under, and they dare not go out on the fishing grounds because of the danger of being run down by these numerous foreign draggers. The same thing is true with respect to their gear. They dare not set their gear because of the danger of having it destroyed by the operation of these draggers. Of course they cannot afford to take the risk. If they once lost their gear they would have no means of replacing it, and their livelihood would be imperilled.
On one occasion it was found that one of these draggers-it was a Spanish dragger named the Santa Amalia-was actually violating the three mile limit. Statements were made to that effect. Affidavits were made by at least two fishermen who took radar bearings on this ship. This particular ship destroyed approximately $350 of gear belonging to one of the fishermen in my riding. We have no recourse. Therefore unless we do something about the 12 mile limit this bill is not going to have very much effect as far as the protection of the coastal fisheries of Newfoundland is concerned.
I know this bill does not define territorial waters. However, the minister and his colleagues must do something about this prob-

lem. The patience of our fishermen is wearing very thin, and the time is going to come before too long when they are going to take the law into their own hands. It would have happened this winter; if they had had the weapons with which to drive these draggers off they would have taken offensive action against them.
Another flaw in the enforcement of this legislation which the minister has put before the house is that we have not the means of enforcing it. We have not sufficient patrol boats to see that even our territorial waters are not violated. The patrol boats we have are small ships 65 feet or 100 feet in length, and they are too small to be out in rough weather. They are all right for rescue work, which they do, and they perform a very good service in that respect; but when it comes to chasing away these foreign draggers they are not at all equal to the task.
Here I want to express my thanks to the minister for all he did this winter in trying to help find a solution to this problem. He sent the Cygnet from Halifax, and at one time he was good enough to work out a plan whereby we had naval ships patrolling these waters. We also had an aerial survey by the Royal Canadian Air Force. However, we must have more and bigger ships if we are going to protect our Newfoundland fisheries. We need about five times as many patrol ships as we have at the present time, and we need ships that are about five times as big.
There is really only one solution to this threat from foreign draggers, and that is to extend our territorial waters out to the 12-mile limit. The minister told us this morning that one section of this act, I think it is section 55, will remove a handicap under which Canadian trawlers now suffer in that Canadian draggers are obliged to fish outside the 12 mile limit while foreign draggers can fish in to the three mile limit. We have no objection to that; we do not want to see our Canadian fishermen deprived of rights which we accord to foreign fishermen. However, it would be better for all concerned if this limit were pushed out to 12 miles offshore, and not only 12 miles following the contour of the coast but 12 miles from headland to headland. We nearly achieved it at the conference at Geneva a year ago; there was only one dissenting vote. But there is no reason why the minister and the government should not work out a convention with those nations which are agreeable to that arrangement of six miles of territorial waters and a further six miles for conservation of fisheries.
We must impress upon the foreign draggers that we mean business in this regard. If we cannot work out a proper agreement

with other nations which should be interested in this problem, the only thing left for us to do is to take unilateral action. I think the government should make it clear that we intend to do that and that we intend to stop pussyfooting in this matter of having foreign draggers encroach and deprive our own fishermen of their livehood.
The other criticism I have to make about this legislation in so far as protection of the fisheries is concerned is that it is designed to protect the fisheries against the little man but that there is in it no means or no machinery to protect them from the big operator. We feel that steps should be taken to deter the big commercial operator. However, the small man-the single man, the inshore fisherman-is the one who is going to be picked up under this legislation. If it is desirable to follow principles of conservation in respect of our fisheries, then it would be more acceptable for this government to take action to establish a 12 mile territorial limit rather than by taking this negative approach.

The
statement made today by the Minister of Fisheries with regard to the amendments that are to be made to the Fisheries Act by Bill No. C-86 will be most welcome to all fishermen on the east coast, and especially to those engaged in deep-sea trawler operations. While there are a number of amendments in this bill, I should like to speak briefly on the 12 mile limit, for in recent years it has become somewhat of a symbol of discrimination by governments against Canada's deep sea fishermen. If all the resolutions passed with regard to this act, and all the speeches that have been made, were placed end to end they would no doubt reach from the Atlantic to the Pacific, for there has been widespread interest in this regulation.
At the recent meeting of the Fisheries Council of Canada, held in Toronto on April 10-12, the following resolution was passed: Whereas Canadian east coast fishing trawlers over 65 feet in length are required by Canadian law to fish outside the 12 mile limit off the mainland east coast, while all foreign fishing boats of any length are permitted to fish within three miles of the Canadian east coast mainland; and Whereas such regulation discriminates against Canadian fishermen;
Therefore be it resolved that the Canadian government be urged to repeal this law at the earliest possible date and give Canadian fishermen the same privileges and fishing rights as are enjoyed by all foreign fishermen.
The wording of this resolution parallels some of the speeches I have made in this house with regard to this problem, and now that the law is to be amended I think it only fitting that the original reasons for this regulation be placed on the record. The best source of information I could find on this subject was the report of the royal commission investigating the fisheries of the maritime provinces and the Magdalen islands, as filed

at Ottawa on May 4, 1928. This is a comprehensive report on all the fisheries problems in the east coast area, but a particular section deals entirely with deep-sea trawlers and their effect on the ground fishing industry.
As most hon. members are aware, a trawler tows a large net or bag about 150 feet in length along the bottom of the sea. The mouth of this huge net is kept open by boards or doors called otter boards, rigged so they operate like kites. Once these trawlers reach the fishing grounds the fishing operation is continuous for at least six or eight days, when the ship returns to port. The net scoops up practically everything on the bottom, from a scallop to a 3,000 pound anchor, along with any fish that may be available; and the immature fish, or those unsuitable for processing and marketing, are thrown back into the sea.
From this brief outline hon. members can readily see that trawler fishing is more wasteful of the fisheries resources than the hook and line method, and it was for this reason that a large number of hook and line fishermen around the turn of the century raised strong objections to the operations of trawlers on the fishing banks.
According to the royal commission report there was only one trawler operating out of Nova Scotia ports in 1910, and between this date and 1927 the number increased to only 10. However, since these trawlers began to operate and dispose of their catch in Canadian markets they have been the subject of keen controversy in the maritime provinces. Their chief opponents were the shore and schooner fishermen who used the hook and trawl line method of catching fish. They argued that the trawlers towing their nets over the bottom destroyed the spawn of the cod and haddock; that they destroyed the feeding grounds of the fish; that they took large quantities of immature and unmarketable fish, causing the inevitable depletion of the fishing grounds; that they destroyed the trawl lines of the fishermen without making restitution; that they market an inferior product, and that they are responsible for over production and consequent glutting of the market, thus preventing the hook and line fishermen from disposing of their catch.
So strong was the protest that on September 9, 1908-and I am quoting from the royal commission report-an order in council was passed providing that "the use or operation of trawlers for the purpose of catching fish is prohibited within the three mile limit of the bays and harbours of Canada". This was obviously an admission that some trawling was injuring the shore fisheries and that it required regulation and restriction. However, 90205-6-267i
Fisheries Act
no changes were made. Protests continued unabated, and on February 5, 1912, with only two trawlers operating from Nova Scotia ports, the minister of marine and fisheries said in the House of Commons:
It is realized that if many steam trawlers are shortly placed in commission on Canadian coasts the hand trawls and long line fishermen will find it hard to compete, and anything that the government can do to protect them, it is anxious to do.
In the meantime protest meetings of fishermen were held in various places, notably in Canso, Lunenburg and Riverport, in Nova Scotia. From a meeting of the deep-sea hook and line fishermen held at Lunenburg on February 9, 1912, a delegation was sent to Ottawa to interview the federal government, with a petition asking that steam trawlers be prohibited from landing their fish in Canada and from obtaining Canadian coal and supplies. Well, that type of resolution would not go down too well today in view of the agitation from Cape Breton to sell more of our coal. However, during the session of 1912, the legislative assembly of Nova Scotia endorsed a resolution to the federal government strongly opposing the operation of trawlers on our east coast. The recommendation made on behalf of the fishermen of Riverport, Nova Scotia, was for prohibition or curtailment of otter trawling, and that a duty be enforced on all fish landed from trawlers of other than Canadian registry.
During the early summer of 1912 a conference was held in Washington attended by representatives of the United States, by the Canadian minister of marine and fisheries and by the prime minister of Newfoundland, as he was then called, with a view to investigating the whole question of steam trawlers and making observations on the results of their operations. After negotiation it was arranged that during the season of 1912 investigations would be carried out by each country independently, with the understanding that upon completion of the work a conference would be held with a view to reaching an agreement for the entire prohibition of trawling on this side of the Atlantic. Meanwhile the war had started, and it was decided to postpone the project and the international conference until the end of the war, but the proposed conference was not held.
In the meantime, in order to protect the hook and trawl line fishermen, the Canadian government in 1915 enacted a regulation under the Customs Act whereby the master of any steam trawler was required, before being granted a clearance for the fishing grounds, to give the customs officer a declaration that he would not fish within 12 miles from the shore. This regulation was to apply

Fisheries Act
to all steam trawlers clearing from a Canadian port on the Atlantic coast. This is the history of the 12 mile limit, and it has been applied since 1915 to the present day.
In fairness to the hook and line fishermen, the objections they raised were valid in their day. They were interested in the conservation of the fisheries. They were concerned with the loss and destruction of their property when trawlers, by day and by night, towed through their trawl lines and destroyed their fishing equipment. They were vitally interested in the serious economic consequences caused by the overproduction of fish by the trawler fishermen and the resultant glut on the market.
Today, however, the situation is considerably changed. The hook and line fisherman setting trawl lines from a dory is almost extinct. The once proud fleet of Bluenose vessels that numbered over 120 at one time out of the port of Lunenburg has now dwindled to a handful. They have been replaced by diesel powered trawlers ranging in size from 65 to 140 feet; by the long-liner which still catches fish on hooks by the use of a long trawl line set astern of the ship; by the gill net fishermen and the Danish seiner. The inshore fisherman is today using at least one of the types of boats I have mentioned, or he may be operating a deep-sea scallop dragger on George's bank, a type of fishing unthought of in 1915. In any event, it is rather ironic that the same areas which made strong representations in 1912 to impose the 12 mile limit on trawlers have been making equally strong representations to this government and to me since I was first elected in 1957 to remove this unfair and restrictive law.
This morning, I listened with interest to the remarks that were made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. He complained about the confining sections of this bill. He said foreign draggers still pose the greatest threat to his inshore fishermen, and mentioned a Spanish trawler in particular. He said the minister and his colleagues must do something about these international trawlers, especially those operating along the coast of Newfoundland.
But I ask, Mr. Speaker, what does he propose? This problem, as I mentioned, has been in existence since the year 1900, when the first trawlers started operating on the east coast. All during the years his party was in office no action was taken. In my opinion, control of these foreign trawlers becomes an international problem. The hon. member further suggested that we extend our territorial waters by unilateral action to the 12 mile limit. This suggestion was supported this afternoon by the hon. member for Skeena.
The statements made by both these hon. members show a remarkable lack of knowledge with regard to our fish marketing problem. I submit that unilateral action of this nature would cause serious repercussions in Canada's export markets, especially in the United States where approximately 80 per cent of our east coast fish production is sold. The New England fisheries association would quickly propose higher tariffs on our fish entering the United States, thereby creating further economic problems for the Atlantic provinces.
We on the east coast, Mr. Speaker, have suffered for 22 years because of this type of Liberal thinking. In my opinion any action taken to extend the east coast fishing limits must be by international agreement. The changes made in the Fisheries Act are a move in the right direction. I know it will meet with genuine approval of the trawler captains operating trawlers on the east coast. I again commend the minister for his foresight in providing Canadian deep-sea fishermen with opportunities equal to those enjoyed by fishermen from other nations.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us to amend the Fisheries Act has some provisions which I think will receive unanimous support in the house and others that will cause questioning. There are some omissions from the bill as well to which the attention of the house, I have no doubt, will be called. Certainly some amendment to the Fisheries Act is overdue. I understand there are some provisions in the present act which have not been changed since 1867, and conditions have changed somewhat since that time.
The bill we have before us was not one mentioned in the speech from the throne as something which was going to be introduced this session. It was not even mentioned last week when the Prime Minister gave the list of legislation which would be brought before the house this session. Perhaps the introduction of the bill at this time can be related to the constructive initiative of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, who introduced a private bill amending the Fisheries Act. Shortly after that, Mr. Speaker, this bill was introduced.
The bill, among other things, does remove some arbitrary powers which are now vested in officials under the act, and that is all to the good. But, as has already been pointed out in this discussion on second reading, the bill does not, in our opinion, go far enough in that respect to establish beyond doubt the principle of innocence until guilt is

proven. However, it does help to bring the existing act into conformity with the bill of rights.
There is one aspect of this bill to which reference has already been made and with which I wish to deal at this time. That is the question of territorial and jurisdictional waters. The bill has some provisions in that regard. It does remove the discrimination now suffered by Canadian draggers as compared with foreign vessels, and that is an improvement. In our view, however, the amendment should have gone further and established a 12 mile zone of jurisdiction enforceable against all vessels, Canadian or foreign.
The hon. member who just preceded me has indicated that this would be a very dangerous course of action to take unilaterally. He was very worried about the repercussions that action of that kind taken by Canada might cause in the United States, and the effect that such action might have on our market for fish in that country, the importance of which of course is recognized by all of us.
The hon. member criticized the Liberal approach to this problem of markets, the approach which I have also just indicated to the establishment of a 12 mile jurisdictional zone. If it had not been for the Liberal approach, implemented by legislation based on international treaty with the United States in 1936, there would not be the present market for Canadian fish in the United States. But the caution displayed by the government in this matter of taking national action to establish a jurisdictional zone, this timidity, if I may put it in that way-certainly was not displayed by the Prime Minister and the members of the present government when they discussed this subject in 1957 and 1958 during the election campaigns. At that time they were all for Canadian action to protect Canadian fisheries interests by the establishment by Canada of a 12 mile fishery zone. I only quote one excerpt from a report-and there are a good many others -of a speech of the Prime Minister on March 26, 1958, appearing in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, when he declared for aid to fishermen and for protection of the rights of Canadian fishermen by a 12 mile limit to be established for all fisheries. That, Mr. Speaker, is what we are asking for now. That is the stand we are taking and have taken as a party since 1957 in respect of this matter.
There are three ways by which Canadian rights over a jurisdictional zone wider than that of the territorial waters zone could be established. In this respect we must, of course, make a distinction between the zone
Fisheries Act
of territorial waters and a jurisdictional zone. Up to the present time we have accepted a three mile territorial zone established on the base line theory, the line from headland to headland, but we believe that beyond the territorial zone, whatever may be its agreed width-and we accept at the present time three miles-there should be a jurisdictional zone especially for fisheries protection and fisheries conservation purposes.
As I have just stated, there are three ways by which this might be done. The first and by far the most satisfactory way of doing it is by international agreement through an international convention. We all know that in recent years efforts have been made at international conferences under United Nations auspices dealing with the law of the sea to get general international agreement on the width of the territorial belt and also of the jurisdictional zone. The present government some time ago-I think it was at the beginning of 1960 or the end of 1959- issued a pamphlet on the law of the sea which explained in detail a Canadian proposal which had been put forward at the Geneva conference for this purpose. That Canadian proposal came to be known as the six plus six theory, and provided for a six mile territorial zone to which would be added a six mile jurisdictional zone, making a belt of 12 miles from the base line over which Canadian law could be exercised. Indeed, that Canadian solution-it really is in effect a 12 mile solution-was put forward, as this pamphlet indicates, as early as the eleventh session of the United Nations general assembly in 1956.
No agreement was reached at the first conference at Geneva with regard to the establishment of any international law of the sea. At the second conference held last year-I think it was in March and April, 1960-a further and very strenuous effort was made to get an acceptable international agreement on this extremely important matter. At that conference, as hon. members know, eventually four proposals were put forward, one by the U.S.S.R., one by Mexico, one by the United States of America and one by Canada. The Mexican and Soviet union proposals were dropped and were replaced, I believe, by an 18-power proposal, while the United States and Canada got together on a compromise one because the difference between their two proposals was not very substantial. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill that is before the house must certainly be received with interest and, generally speaking, with approval because of its attempts to reform long existing legislation. However, its very nature and importance, particularly to us from the seaboard districts, are such that it does require very careful scrutiny by this house.
The bill is obviously intended to rectify existing legislation and bring it more into line with modern needs and thinking. In so far as it deals with pollution I think the suggested amendments are good, because under the old act the penalties were so light that a big operator could, if he wished, break the law with impunity. There are teeth in these amendments, teeth which I think should be there.
With respect to some of the penalties, however, particularly the seizure of gear, I agree with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, who pointed out that if a fisherman broke the law and his traps or nets were seized, he would be placed in a position where he would automatically be unable to earn a livelihood. For instance, if the nets which he used to catch bait were taken, his whole fishing season could be ruined.
Therefore it occurs to me that a very careful second look should be given to this matter of penalties and the type of penalties which should be exacted. We should carefully consider whether or not fishing gear or fishing property should be automatically confiscated upon guilt being proved. We should consider whether a fine or imprisonment should be instituted in place of confiscation, because there is no doubt that the confiscation of property can work real hardship, not only on the guilty party but on his fishing partners, his associates and his family. The actual penalty might in fact be far out of proportion to the crime committed, because the property or gear seized might be worth only a few hundred dollars but if it means the loss of a season's work it runs into much more money than that.
I am sure the minister and all of us want the punishment to fit the crime. In saying that, I should like to make it clear that I understand the necessity of making sure that the punishment does fit the crime and is not too light, because unless the Minister of Fisheries were in a position to enforce the
Fisheries Act
acts which are necessary for the conservation of the fisheries, the whole purpose of these fisheries regulations would be defeated; and without proper protection, certain fisheries may in time cease to exist.
Therefore in asking for a new look to be given to the penalty part of this bill I am not suggesting that flagrant violations of the law with regard to conservation should be overlooked. Rather I am trying to point out, if it is necessary for it to be pointed out, the desirability of having a punishment for violations whereby teeth could be kept in the regulations but it would not be necessary to cause undue and prolonged hardship to the person affected.
There is the matter of enforcing the regulations and the patrol of coastal waters. I agree with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, who appealed for more and larger vessels, but I go a step further than that. I do not think it would be economic to maintain the number of vessels which would be required to adequately protect the coastal waters of Canada. The Department of Fisheries would have to have its own navy. Well, they have one now, and a very good one. However, I think you would pretty soon, get into the law of diminishing returns if you built enough ships to patrol all the coastal waters of Canada. I do suggest that we should have more and larger patrol ships we should have patrol which can stay at sea in bad weather, as some fishing ships can. As the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) pointed out, more of these ships are certainly needed.
In addition, I would suggest an increase in the amount of air patrolling. At the present time I believe there is a limited air patrol carried out by the Department of Fisheries. I do think it would be highly desirable and highly effective if an air patrol were maintained off the coast of Canada. In this connection I think that the search and rescue unit of the R.C.A.F. which is already established at Torbay, for instance, as well as in other places, could provide such an air patrol or supplement the air patrol carried out by the Department of Fisheries. Such a patrol, working in conjunction with an adequate inspection fleet would do much to protect the waters off our coast.
Now we come to a subject to which reference has already been made by a number of speakers. I think the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, and the hon. member for Queens-Lunenberg (Mr. Crouse) have each referred to the question of the 12 mile limit. I agree completely with what was said by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon.

Fisheries Act
member for Burin-Burgeo. I disagree completely with the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg who seems to think that all the ills affecting the fisheries are due to Liberal thinking. The hon. member was using the word "Liberal" with a political connotation. I would say, using the word "liberal" in another sense, that we have been much too liberal in allowing foreign fishing vessels the free use of our territorial waters.
The presence of a Russian icebreaker equipped with helicopters to fly sealers into the ice fields off our coast this year is perhaps of more direct significance for Canada than the Russians having the first man in space. Certainly the waters off Newfoundland, Labrador, Nova Scotia and our west coast are Canadian waters and their use affects not only individual provinces but all provinces. I should like to strongly support the suggestion- made that Canada should have a 12 mile limit from point to point and that this 12 mile limit should be strictly enforced. This can be done.
As I have said on many occasions, the presence in our waters of so many ships belonging to our foreign competitors is bound to have an adverse effect upon our own direct interests and the growth of competition makes it highly desirable that Canada should take steps to preserve the rich waters off our coasts for her own use and for the benefit of her own citizens.

have only a few words to add to the very interesting debate on this bill. I am chiefly concerned with section 64, or, to be more precise with section 64(a) of the act. I wish to draw the attention of the house and of the minister to what I consider to be something which may cause discrimination in the enforcement.
The hon. member who has just spoken emphasized the hardship caused by confiscation after seizure. Well, in some cases confiscation is necessary. My concern relates to the confiscation of goods when the owner is innocent or when the identity of the owner has not been ascertained. Under the bill, if a person is charged and defends himself, and is then convicted, the owner, if he is not the accused person, has 30 days after the conviction in which to make application to a judge for an order to have his equity protected.
However, on the other hand if at the time of the seizure no one is charged and the owner of the goods is not identified there is only a period of 30 days allowed. I hope that when the bill is in the committee stage the minister will give some consideration to extending the period of 30 days allowed for making an application for protection to a judge.

I am mainly concerned about goods owned by an innocent person for example after a theft. When goods have been stolen they can be used illegally or improperly by the thief and the innocent owner might not know of the offence until the period of 30 days had expired.

was interested in the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) regarding the unilateral establishment of a 12 mile limit. I am thinking, now, especially in terms of the Pacific coast. I think we should all like to see it, but there are some difficulties in establishing this limit unilaterally because of the nature of the boundaries between British Columbia and the United States. Such difficulties will arise particularly in such places as the straits of San Juan which in many areas are considerably less than 24 miles in width, in the neighbourhood of Hecate strait between the Queen Charlotte islands and the mainland, and along the southern part of what we call the Alaskan Panhandle.
I cannot see how we can establish a 12 mile limit unilaterally. I think it would have to be done by bilateral agreement. I believe that any attempt to establish such a limit unilaterally would result in a great controversy between ourselves and the United States and would inevitably result in bloodshed. I think the United States fishermen would resist an attempt to enforce such a boundary unilaterally in the same way as our fishermen would resist it in areas where a unilateral United States definition of a 12 mile limit was not in their interests.
I should therefore like to suggest to the Leader of the Opposition that his remarks apply with more force to the Atlantic coast. His suggestion might be feasible there-it might be practical-but I think if we were to try it unilaterally on the Pacific coast we would be asking for a lot more trouble than we could handle.
