speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not intend to detain the house very long on this bill because, as hon. members will all appreciate, I make no claim to skill or knowledge as a fisherman, at least as far as sea fishing is concerned. The closest acquaintance with the art of fishing that I can claim-and it has been a very pleasant one -is, of course, by way of fly fishing, and perhaps I could take this opportunity to put in a boost for that splendid domestic fish known as the Kamloops trout, the finest sport fish in North America.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I recognize, however, that this bill does not concern this branch of the art, and that it relates mainly to problems of no concern to inland fisheries.
I wish to take part in the debate for two specific reasons. First, I want to deal with some remarks which have been made as to the incidents surrounding the introduction of the bill. Second, I wish to deal with the understandable concern and interest of hon. members in the relationship between this bill and the provisions of the bill of rights.
First, with respect to the circumstances of the introduction of the bill; it has been suggested by some hon. members that the bill may have been introduced because of an attempt made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) to introduce and proceed with a private bill of his own. Let me assure the house that is far from correct. While we in this government do pay a good deal of regard to private members and their views, and are always anxious to obtain the benefit of their views, in this situation, while appreciating the interest of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, let me assure you that the bill now before the house was in preparation long before that purported bill of his saw the light of day.
This bill was in preparation in the Department of Fisheries last fall and has been considered in detail in my department, in the context of the bill of rights, as far back as last December.
Indeed it would be, in large part, correct to say that one of the main reasons for the introduction of the present bill was the concern of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) with respect to the situation in which he and his officers found themselves under the present Fisheries Act as a result of the bill of rights. I can assure the house that my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries is, as are all members of the present government, most careful to review the legislation and the activities of the officers for which he is responsible to ensure that the legislation does not place him or his officers in a position where things are likely to be done contrary to the bill of rights. It was because of the concern of my colleague with regard to this matter-that was one of the main reasons-that he sought approval for the introduction of this bill to revise the Fisheries Act.
As has been pointed out by all of those hon. members who have spoken on this bill, it is a tremendous improvement, with respect to this kind of matter, over the Fisheries Act as it is presently. I should like to remind the hon. members of this house, when they are considering and recalling to their minds some of the things that were said at the time of the debate on the bill of rights-
Fisheries Act
that it would be of no effect, was nothing but words, and other suggestions made by members of the opposition-that we have here before us today a very concrete example of the effectiveness of the bill of rights. When you see the extent to which the Fisheries Act, a statute which has been on the books for many years, has offended the provisions of the present bill of rights, you will understand the important step forward made in introducing this piece of legislation entirely in conformity with that bill of rights.
I am not going to attempt to go far enough back into history to assess particular responsibilities for these objectionable features in the present Fisheries Act, but I do point out to you that our predecessors had 22 years of opportunity to remove them but did nothing about it, yet within a very short time of the passage of the bill of rights by this government we have this concrete example of the seriousness with which, under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), human rights and fundamental freedoms are observed.
I do not propose to go into a long dissertation at this point on the matter of the due process of law, which is that portion of the bill of rights of main concern in connection with the enforcement provisions of the Fisheries Act, but I do want to assure the house in general that I have been at pains to satisfy myself that this bill is in conformity with the bill of rights in every respect. Something has been said here with regard to the report of the Minister of Justice in respect of the bill of rights which leads me to believe that it may be well to outline to the house again the procedure that is to be followed in connection with ascertaining that legislation introduced in this house is not contrary to the spirit and provision of this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The problem of enforcement of fisheries legislation from the point of view of the bill of rights arises largely out of the fact that there are some pieces of fisheries equipment which are used for illegal purposes which, if not disposed of promptly, will in fact carry out that illegal purpose to the prejudice of the general public. It therefore becomes desirable to provide a method under which the offending equipment may be disposed of immediately in order that the public interest may be protected. It is in connection with the devising of a procedure that gives a speedy method of disposal, but which at the same time does not arbitrarily deprive an individual of his rights, that the problem arises. And it is that specific problem that the new draft bill before us has met and, in my view, has met fairly and successfully.
Under the old Fisheries Act it is true that wide powers of forfeiture on view were given to fisheries officers, with the result that where a fisheries officer felt that an offence was being committed, he had wide powers of seizure resulting in an automatic and complete forfeiture of the goods in question.
I should go on to say that an owner, even an innocent owner, had no recourse against such a forfeiture. I use the word "innocent" to describe an owner whose goods might have been used without his permission or knowledge for the offensive purpose; even that owner had no recourse against the complete forfeiture to the crown, which resulted from the unilateral action, without a hearing, on the part of the fisheries officer. Of course, Mr. Speaker, it is essential that that situation should be remedied and it has been remedied in the bill now before you.
The scheme of the present bill is that in general there should be no forfeiture without a hearing. The article with which the offence is alleged to have been committed must be ordered to be forfeited by a court under proceedings to be brought by the minister. It is true that the present bill does authorize fisheries officers to seize, and this seizure would have the effect of forfeiture if nothing else were done. It is provided here that since the forfeiture itself can only be ordered by the court, an owner shall not be effectively deprived of the right to his prop-perty by the minister refraining from bringing action. Hon. members will appreciate that
Fisheries Act
if the article is seized and nothing is done, the owner would otherwise be effectively deprived of possession. Therefore, we go on to provide that unless the minister brings action within three months from the date of seizure the goods shall be restored to their owner. In other words, if the minister finds that he has not got a case, or that the seizure was made in error, then he cannot simply let the matter drop and effectively deprive someone of his rights. If he does not bring action within three months the goods are automatically restored. As I say-
Will the minister explain how that boat and equipment are going to catch fish while they are confiscated for three months?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am endeavouring to explain the scheme under which this very difficult problem of enforcement and of protection of the fisheries in the public interest has been resolved. It is true that with respect to one class of fisheries equipment there can be a forfeiture without the owner having been in effect notified, and that is in connection with lobster pots. My understanding is that frequently lobster pots are found out in the sea, in an area in which lobster fishing is prohibited, or in an area at a time when the lobster season is closed.
Those lobster pots are, of course, actually being used for an offence and there is not much point in leaving them there while the fisheries officer goes back to court. Further lobsters will crawl into the pots while the fisheries officer is off in court; the offender may come and remove them while his back is turned. Therefore, it is provided with respect to this particular item of fishing equipment that it may be forfeited and disposed of immediately as the minister directs.
However, it is further provided in the next proposed section that if there is an owner who is an innocent owner even of items in this class, he may within 30 days make application to the court, and if he establishes that the property was his and that it was being used without his knowledge or consent, then he is entitled to the return of his property, or, if it has already been disposed of, to the return of the equivalent value. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think it will be generally agreed that in view of the really difficult problems of enforcement that exist, the scheme that has been devised is one which is reasonable and which protects the public interest without prejudice to the rights of individuals as they are declared in the bill of rights.
As I have said, I do not want to go into a long dissertation on this question of "due process", although it was around this point

Fisheries Act
that the main difficulty revolved namely, are we depriving people of their rights without due process of law? We have done some research on it and the house may be interested in a brief summary of the position. It will be appreciated, of course, that in connection with this phrase "the due process of law" there is not much jurisprudence in Canada, nor is there, indeed, in the United Kingdom. The main jurisprudence is found in the United States. While I do not suggest for a moment that the United States cases will serve as binding precedents, I certainly think it is not unlikely and not unreasonable that our courts would turn to examine the views of the courts in the United States to see what has been the thinking on this subject and the interpretation given to the due process section. Therefore, I think the house might be interested in a summary of one of the leading cases in the United States on this question.
I refer to the case of Lawton versus Steele in 1893, reported at 38 United States supreme court reports at page 385. It is interesting to note that this case arose out of a fisheries statute of the state of New York, which contained the following provision:
Any net, pound, or other means or device for taking or capturing fish, or whereby they may be taken or captured, set, put, floated, had, found, or maintained, in or upon any of the waters of this state, or upon the shores of or islands in any of the waters of this state, in violation of any existing or hereafter enacted statutes or laws for the protection of fish is hereby declared to be, and is, a public nuisance, and may be abated and summarily destroyed by any person, and it shall be the duty of each and every protector aforesaid and of every game constable to seize and remove and forthwith destroy the same,... and no action for damages shall lie or be maintained against any person for or on account of any such seizure and destruction.
This provision was attacked and alleged to be unconstitutional and void for the reason, amongst others, that it deprived a citizen of his property without due process of law. In coming to its decision, the court said as follows:
The extent and limits of what is known as the police power have been a fruitful subject of discussion in the appellate courts of nearly every state in the union. It is universally conceded to include everything essential to the public safety, health, and morals, and to justify the destruction or abatement, by summary proceedings, of whatever may be regarded as a public nuisance.
Perhaps I should pause here to observe, Mr. Speaker, that although we do not have the doctrine of police power developed in the same precise form as is the case in the United States, nevertheless it is apparent to all hon. members that powers of enforcement such as are contained in this bill rest on the doctrine of police power, namely that the governments, on behalf of the public, must do those things which are necessary and have

a right to provide legislative sanction for the doing of those things which are necessary for the protection of the public interest. However, all jurisdictions under our system of democracy have recognized, and it is inherent in the bill of rights, that the state cannot rely on the doctrine of police power to go so far as arbitrarily to deprive a citizen of what are his fundamental rights without due process of law.
The supreme court of the United States which, as I said, is a country where this whole problem of reconciling police power with individual rights has been exhaustively considered by the courts, went on to say this:
... To justify the state in thus interposing its authority in behalf of the public, it must appear, first, that the interests of the public generally, as distinguished from those of a particlular class, require such interference; and, second, that the means are reasonably necessary for the accomplishment of the purpose, and not unduly oppressive upon individuals. The legislature may not, under the guise of protecting the public interests, arbitrarily interfere with private business, or impose unusual and unnecessary restrictions upon lawful occupations. In other words, its determination as to what is a proper exercise of its police powers is not final or conclusive, but is subject to the supervision of the courts.
I pause here to interpolate that under our bill of rights we have assured that provisions enacted by the legislature here are similarly subject to the supervision of the courts.
The judgment continues:
*-the preservation of game and fish, however, has always been treated as within the proper domain of the police power, and laws limiting the season within which birds and wild animals may be killed or exposed for sale, and prescribing the time and manner in which fish may be caught, have been repeatedly upheld by the courts.
The court then turned its attention to the act in question of New York state from which I have read and which, as I have pointed out, went so far as to say that any net, pound, or other means or device for taking or capturing fish, and being used in violation of any existing or hereafter enacted statute of the state, is a public nuisance, and may be seized and summarily destroyed. It was that provision to which the supreme court of the United States turned its attention, and they said this:
The main, and only real difficulty connected with the act in question is in its declaration that any net, etc., maintained in violation of any law for the protection of fisheries, is to be treated as a public nuisance, "and may be abated and summarily destroyed by any person, and it shall be the duty of each and every protector aforesaid and every game constable to seize, remove and forthwith destroy the same." The legislature, however, undoubtedly possessed the power not only to prohibit fishing by nets in these waters, but to make it a criminal offence, and to take such measures as were reasonable and necessary to prevent such offences in the future. It certainly could not do

this more effectually than by destroying the means of the offence. If the nets were being used in a manner detrimental to the interests of the public, we think it was within the power of the legislature to declare them to be nuisances, and to authorize the officers of the state to abate them.
Then, sir, the supreme court of the United States turned to a problem which has exercised us here. We have provided in the present bill that large items of property, expensive items, where either the value of the property or the ease of determining ownership, or both, make it patently absurd to provide a situation where they could be ordered to be forfeited simply because somebody says he cannot identify the owner-we have provided that shall not take place without a hearing in so far as fishing vessels or vehicles are concerned, and a determination must be made of the issue of whether or not an offence has been committed with such articles, at which time an innocent owner may be given an opportunity to come in.
However, in the case of these small items of the class I have mentioned, this problem is much more difficult. It is highly likely there will be no trace of ownership, no means of identification in the first place. In the second place, if they are being used to commit an offence, and they are of small value, then obviously no one is going to identify them because by so doing he renders himself liable to the penalty for committing the offence. Therefore, there will be no one coming along and claiming ownership, so the only practical result is that ownership may be forfeited by the very commission of the offence.
The supreme court of the United States said this in respect of this matter:
But where the property is of little value, and its use for the illegal purpose is clear, the legislature may declare it to be a nuisance, and subject to summary abatement. Instances of this are the power to kill diseased cattle: to pull down houses in the path of conflagration; destruction of decayed fruit or fish or unwholesome meats, or infected clothing, obscene books or pictures, or instruments which can only be used for illegal purposes. While the legislature has no right arbitrarily to declare that to be a nuisance which is clearly not so, a good deal must be left to its discretion in that regard, and if the object to be accomplished is conducive to the public interests, it may exercise a large liberty of choice in the means employed.
Finally, I should like to put this passage before the house dealing with items of this class:
The value of the nets in question was but $15 apiece. The cost of condemning one, (and the use of one is as illegal as the use of a dozen) by judicial proceedings, would largely exceed the value of the net, and doubtless the state would in many cases, be deterred from executing the law by the expense. They could only be removed from the water with difficulty, and were liable to injury in the process of removal. The object of the law is undoubtedly a beneficent one, and the
Fisheries Act
state ought not to be hampered in its enforcement, by the application of constitutional provisions which are intended for the protection of substantial rights of property. It is evidence that the efficacy of this statute would be very seriously impaired by requiring every net illegally used to be carefully taken from the water, carried before a court or magistrate, notice of the seizure to be given by publication, and regular judicial proceedings to be instituted for its condemnation.
That case is not exactly similar to all the cases that may arise under this legislation, but it is interesting I think to see something of the general approach which the highest court in the United States took to this matter, a court very much seized with the importance of human rights and fundamental freedoms. It is interesting because in the general discussion, parts of which I have read here, they dealt extensively with this problem of the proper exercise of the police power, proper protection of the public interest on the one hand, as against the protection of individual property rights on the other.
So, Mr. Speaker, I say to the house through you that, in the drafting of this legislation, we have been scrupulously careful to ensure that every reasonable protection-and indeed more than reasonable protection-is given to property rights of the individual and that where it is physically and practically feasible to do so within the confines of an effective enforcement measure, no arbitrary powers of confiscation, seizure or forfeiture are given and no one is liable to have his property taken from him and disposed of without the right to a hearing and to defend his rights and his interests.
As I said, the bill was reviewed from this point of view in our department from as far back as last December. It has been examined by me in that process and I have no report to make to the house as to any inconsistency with the bill of rights. May I remind the house that, under the bill of rights, my obligation is to report inconsistencies; it is not my obligation to make a general report if I find no inconsistencies. Therefore, if there is no report that means that no inconsistency has been found. In every case, of course, a copy is required to be deposited with the Clerk bearing a certificate that it has been examined in the Department of Justice. That is required under regulations worked out between my department and Mr. Speaker for the efficient information of the house under the terms of the bill of rights. So that in so far as concerns the suggestion that an official report from the Minister of Justice is expected with respect to every piece of legislation, may I say that is not the approach that is taken. What is required from the Minister of Justice by the statute is a report if he finds inconsistencies between a piece of legislation and

Fisheries Act
the bill of rights; and in my view, there are no such inconsistencies in this bill.
May I ask the minister a question-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

-or may I ask two questions? One is this. Did he find no inconsistencies in Bill No. C-76? What is the purpose of this report which he is required to make under standing order 40 if it is not to guide the house in the framing of amendments to take care of inconsistencies?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Your Honour has already ruled that a discussion on the process by which I arrive at my opinion is out of order and also has suggested that a discussion of Bill No. C-76 and whether or not it is in conformity with the bill of rights is not in order in a debate on this bill. This morning I commenced to indicate my opinion of Bill No. C-76 and the Speaker stopped me. This afternoon I have pointed out that with respect to Bill No. C-76, in the explanatory note and in the explanation that the hon. member gave when he introduced it, it was said to be a bill for the purpose of revising the Fisheries Act and bringing it into conformity with the bill of rights. However, the bill as drafted does nothing of the sort. It merely re-enacts the Fisheries Act. I do not think I should go any further in the course of this debate.

Your Honour or Mr. Speaker said I would have an opportunity to contradict a statement or to correct a statement that the minister made. The minister has just now made another statement that is wrong and I want to quote-

Speaking to a point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I believe the intent was that the hon. member would correct it in committee or at some succeeding place in the debate. He has already spoken on second reading. It is my understanding that an hon. member can speak only once on second reading.
Speaking to the point of order may I say that it is common practice and within the rules to make a correction immediately after a misstatement has been made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Of course the hon. member may correct a statement made by another hon. member if the statement refers to what the hon. member has said and is a misinterpretation of what he said. If the hon. member wishes to rise and take the opportunity at the end of a speech, he may do so. But this is not the situation. The hon. member may not rise only to correct a statement of fact made by another hon. member. It

must refer to what he said. If that is the purpose of the hon. member I will give him the floor.

That is right Mr. Speaker. I wish to correct a statement which the minister made just before he took his seat. I want to quote from the explanatory note in my bill just one sentence as follows:
The purposes of this bill.. . therefore are:
1. To determine whether any of the provisions of this bill are inconsistent with the Canadian bill of rights: in particular, the provisions of clause 35 which empower a fishery officer to accuse a person of violating the fisheries laws and then to adjudicate on that person's guilt or innocence;
I could quote more but I think I have quoted enough to correct the statement the minister just made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What the hon. member has quoted, far from correcting what I have said, confirms what I have said.
I think this discussion is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
For the guidance of hon. members I think perhaps I should read standing order 37 which states as follows:
No member may speak twice to a question except in explanation of a material part of his speech which may have been misquoted or misunderstood, but then he is not to introduce any new matter and no debate shall be allowed upon such explanation.
I therefore think we should close the matter at that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With respect, Mr. Speaker, may I point out that the hon. member rose by way of a question first. Then the matter of Bill No. C-76 had been included in the comments made this afternoon. Then the hon. member commented on something I had said, and as he put it, he corrected me. I am simply seeking to point out that his bill when it is examined, clearly does not do what he says is its purpose. What it does is to re-enact the Fisheries Act, the very piece of legislation to which he says he has objections.
A successful breach of the rules.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the passage of this important bill. However, because of the importance of our fisheries to our great dominion and because I represent one of the most important fishing industries and fishing communities in Canada I feel that I cannot allow the occasion to pass without saying a few words in support of the bill. In our fish industry we have a Klondike which is just as great as any gold claim that has ever been utilized or sold in California. Every year there are caught off our coasts both east

and west millions of dollars worth of fish of all descriptions. Reference has been made to this bill, to what the Liberal government did not do and to what it should have done. In my opinion for what it is worth, this bill was brought about because of the bill which was introduced by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter).
Nonsense.

The fact that the Liberal government did not do anything to improve the conditions about which the Progressive Conservative government feels something should be done, does not excuse it for not doing anything. We are glad to see that steps have been taken by the Progressive Conservative government to improve our fisheries.
There are two important factors that are to be considered in connection with this bill. One is the enforcement of the fishing regulations and the other is the protection of our fisheries against foreign powers.
If we have not sufficient vessels to see that our rights are protected, I think this government or any government should take steps to see that the necessary protection is given to this important industry.
It seems to me that our officials are more concerned with enforcing the law upon our own fishermen than they are in seeing it enforced upon foreigners.
Last year I asked a question of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean). My question is reported at page 2123 of Hansard for 1960:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. Has his attention been called to a report that a foreign sealing vessel is operating within the territorial waters of Canada and, if so, what action is his department taking?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, a telegram has been received in which the sender says it was reported to him that a foreign sealing vessel was operating within Canadian territorial waters.
The minister added that he had taken immediate steps to investigate the situation. At that time the minister had not received a report from his officers, but later he did receive a report and a plane was sent out to investigate the incident. Because of the type of investigation carried out, no grounds were found for the complaint.
I have here a flag which was taken from a vessel within the three mile limit. It is not the type of flag about which we have heard so much political propaganda in the house recently, but it was taken from a sealer and it is of foreign origin.
It is a red flag.

It is a red flag, not a blue one. This brings me to the question of the 12 mile limit. Previous speakers have said they fear
Fisheries Act
what would take place if Canada were to put real teeth into the regulations to enforce a 12 mile limit.
I should like to read from an editorial in a recent issue of the Evening Telegram of St. John's:
Just over two years ago the government and the people of Iceland became very concerned about their livelihood, especially the portion that depends on the fisheries.
Whereupon Iceland, unilaterally, i.e. ''on her own hook", without consultation with any other maritime nation or world organization, extended her traditional three mile fishing limit to 12. This was vigorously opposed by Britain, an ancient friend of Iceland, which has been sending fishing ships to Icelandic waters since the Middle Ages. But Iceland was stubborn; there were incidents when her patrol vessels interfered with British draggers; at one stage British men-o-war went along as escorts.
After 13 years of the arbitrary establishment of fishing limits Iceland has agreed to proposals that future disputes should come under the jurisdiction of the international court of justice.
These proposals, which were published recently in London, provide for the immediate recognition by Britain of Iceland's 12 mile limit, with a three year phase out during which British vessels would be allowed to fish in certain areas up to six miles from amended base lines.
The case of Britain and Iceland shows that the latter did not lose her ancient friend, but instead won recognition of the vital nature of her own valuable fisheries.
As soon as we have the courage to state where we stand and look after our fisheries, I think the better off we will be.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief comments on this bill. I agree with what the bill tries to do in general. How well it does this I suppose we will be able to discuss at the committee stage.
Like many other hon. members of this house, I believe that this bill has been hurried in its presentation because of the bill which has been given first reading and which was presented to the house by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter). I commend the hon. member for the remarks he has made and for his efforts to have the Fisheries Act amended in order to bring it up ro date to meet present-day requirements.
Like many other hon. members of the house, I am a little bit concerned about the penalties to be imposed upon these poor fishermen. I speak with some knowledge of this matter because of those with whom I have had some dealings.
The type of thing that bothers me is this Let us take the case of a fisherman who is accused of committing an offence under the

Fisheries Act
Fisheries Act, whose fishing gear is taken away from him and who is afterwards found to be innocent; or perhaps after a period of three months it is decided to take no action and his gear is returned to him.
If we are talking about the lobster industry in Newfoundland, the salmon industry, or to a large extent the cod fishery, by the end of those three months the period in which this man could have made a living has expired. I think that preventing such a man from making a summer's wages, or a season's wages, as the case may be, imposes a very severe penalty upon him for an offence which he may not have committed.
Another thing that bothers me about this question is this. A man may have committed an offence under the act. I hold no brief for those who commit offences under the act; they should receive the full penalty of the law. But if a man has committed an offence under the act and has been punished by order of the court, must he also be punished by suffering loss of wages due to his fishing gear having been taken away from him?
Perhaps when we reach the committee stage on this bill we will hear from the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) as to how this particular situation can be prevented. I believe that this question of the penalties to be imposed upon fishermen needs to be examined very closely.
This bill also makes reference to the protection of fisheries. I wish to refer for a moment or two to the protection of inland fisheries. I am referring particularly to sport fishing in Newfoundland. In the section of Newfoundland from which I come sport fishing brings to the area a large number of tourists every year, and has done so for more than half a century.
We feel that sport fishing is the attraction which brings so many tourists to our part of the province. We hope protection will be given to the inland fisheries so that sport fishing can be conserved for the future and will remain a drawing card for people to come to the province of Newfoundland during the warmer periods of the year. I feel that at the moment insufficient protection is being given to this particular industry.
I believe more guardians are needed on the rivers to see that the fisheries are protected. I believe, also, that they should begin their work before the season opens and that they should remain at work for a period after the season closes. I am going to suggest now -and I intend to do so again when the estimates of the minister are before the committee of the whole-that a complete survey

should be undertaken to determine what conservation and protection measures are required to safeguard the fishing of the west coast of Newfoundland and that having made such a determination we should carry out the protection measures required at the earliest possible date.
Coming from Newfoundland, or from the Atlantic provinces, I am, of course, concerned about fishing limits. On numerous occasions fishermen have told me that foreign draggers are fishing well within the three mile limit. I have no knowledge of this personally but neither have I any reason to doubt the stories that these fishermen have told me. We on the west coast of Newfoundland- and this may well apply to other parts of the province-have a situation where four or five miles off the coast there exists a fishing shoal, a fishing bank or fishing grounds. Fishermen from the nearby communities have fished these grounds for years and years.
In many cases the people who live in the nearby settlements have to depend upon these grounds for their livelihood; they find that they are their only means of employment. Yet draggers from foreign countries will come and in one season drag these grounds so that they are no longer able to provide a living for the number of men who have to live in the area. I recognize that some of these grounds are outside the three mile limit. Nevertheless, these foreign draggers are destroying the means which these people have of making a living and I suggest this is a matter which deserves very serious attention.
I regret the fact that in discussing these things today some of our speakers have got a little bit political. That might not be a good thing today as far as Newfoundland is concerned. Some of the things which have been spoken of here were all done by this parliament before Newfoundland came into the picture and if we were to go back further we should find that Newfoundland, in trying to solve her fishing problems, was not very well served by the federal government at a time when a Conservative government was in office.
Of course, you are not being political now.

I am doing exactly what you were doing. I think we could have discussed this bill and left all these things out, especially as there is agreement-
Mr. Graff fey: Your objectivity floors me.

I am not concerned about you. I would be enhancing the value of that remark unduly if I called it stupid.

Last year during the debate on external affairs I had some comments to make about the 12 mile limit and I believe the time is coming when Canada will have to make some decision about this question. There is no need here to make any further observations as to the importance of the fishing industry to Canada as a nation but I think one thing we should never forget is that when we are talking about the importance of an industry to the nation as a whole it is sometimes wise to pay attention to the importance of that industry to a particular region. An industry may not be especially important to Canada as a whole but it may nevertheless be of total importance to one small region. I think we sometimes have to view an industry in that way.
In the last few years world production of fish has increased by about 35 per cent while the total production by Canada has remained about the same. An odd thing about this is that the increase in world fisheries production, or a large percentage of it, has been taken from the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of Canada. In order adequately to preserve the fisheries in the northwest Atlantic I believe it is necessary for this country to institute fishing limits. These limits have been discussed internationally in the past. There was the Hague conference of 1930 and there was the Geneva conference in 1958, and while the Geneva conference in 1958 might not have arrived at the conclusion which we would have liked so far as territorial and fishing limits are concerned I would not infer from that that this conference was a failure. Far from it. I think it laid some very important groundwork upon which fishing limits can be based.
Then there was the conference of 1960. I think it was unfortunate that Canada came so close to having its contention acknowledged; it was unfortunate that the proposition which the Canadian delegation placed before the convention was not voted on in such a manner as to bring it to a successful conclusion.
I am wondering what could be done failing international agreement among all the nations who took part in that conference of 1960. Of the 87 nations represented at that conference, 54 voted in favour of the Canadian proposition, 28 voted against and five abstained. If it is not possible for all the countries represented at that conference to arrive at some conclusion, I am wondering if it would not be possible to have some agreement reached between those nations which voted for the Canadian proposition in 1960. I recognize that this would not constitute an international agreement but it may
Fisheries Act
be we shall find that reaching an international agreement on this question is going to take a lot of time if, indeed, it can ever be done.
In the meantime the failure of these countries to reach agreement is producing a reaction on our fishing industry which none of us wishes to see. As I say, it may be that one thing we could do would be to attempt to reach agreement with the 54 nations voting for the Canadian proposition. If that is not possible, perhaps it would be possible to arrive at some agreement between the nations which now fish in the northwest Atlantic. If this cannot be done I would have to agree that perhaps the only course we could take would be to declare unilaterally a 12 mile limit around the coast of Canada.
If every other proposition fails I think that is what Canada should do. There are many other nations in the world which have declared their fishing limits unilaterally, some of them recently and some of them years ago. In 1906 Norway declared a fishing limit of four miles. Last year Norway declared that her fishing limits would be increased to 12 miles according to a statement made by the foreign minister of Norway after the Geneva conference of 1960.
Let us examine the unilateral declarations made by other nations and the years they were established. In 1907, Argentine, 12 miles; in 1909, Spain, 6 miles; 1912, Italy, 7 miles; 1914, Greece, 6 miles; 1923, Colombia, 12 miles; 1933, Ecuador, 15 miles; 1938, Brazil, 12 miles; 1949, Costa Rica, 200 miles; 1951, Korea, 50 to 60 miles; 1952, the Dominican Republic, 12 miles; 1955, El Salvador, 200 miles; India, 100 miles and Ceylon, 100 miles. I have taken these figures from a table provided by the secretariat of the United Nations in 1958 when this discussion, in which I was particularly interested, took place in that organization.
If other nations have been able to extend unilateral fishing limits, and if no other method is found to solve our own problems, I would suggest Canada will have to declare unilaterally a 12 mile fishing limit. I recognize immediately that if we should do so many problems will arise regarding our relations with other nations, particularly the United States, in respect of our markets for fish. I believe, however, if Canada were to declare a unilateral 12 mile fishing limit it would be possible to enter into agreement with those other nations which are particularly concerned with Canadian fishing limits. I see no reason why we cannot enter into bilateral agreements with other countries in order to protect their interests while, at the same time, protecting our own markets.

Fisheries Act
I recognize that by declaring a fishing limit we give rise to various problems, particularly the patrolling of that area inside the limits. I believe that a solution can be found, that most countries would be willing to recognize Canada's fishing resources, and that protection must be given them. If no other method is found to solve this problem then I would suggest that a declaration of a unilateral 12 mile limit must be made.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Would the hon. member suggest that the 12 mile limit off the coast of British Columbia would be measured from Vancouver or the west coast of the Queen Charlotte islands? What does he contemplate in this situation?

I would not be able to provide a good answer to that question. All the references I have made this afternoon have had regard to that portion of Canada with which I am familiar, namely, the east coast. I realize that fisheries on the west coast of Canada are very important to the people there, but I would not, with my limited knowledge of the coast of British Columbia, be able to decide just how the 12 mile limit should be imposed, whether it should follow the contour of the land or follow a line adjoining the headlands. I would think that hon. members from ridings on the west coast could certainly present some solution to the problem.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is particularly important to residents of British Columbia because of the fact that approximately half of the commercial fish in Canada are caught there.
The development and control of fisheries is a function of government. In respect of inland waters this is a responsibility of the provincial government; in respect of coastal waters, it is a responsibility of the federal government. Since our fisheries are almost entirely coastal water fisheries, and involve the great streams emptying into the Pacific coast-still salt water fisheries-the control is a responsibility of the federal government. In view of this situation any advancement in respect of this industry is dependent upon the action taken by the federal government.
Many of the changes proposed to the Fisheries Act have been requested during the past two years by representatives of that industry. I believe this proposed bill will meet the needs of those representatives. It may be of interest to hon. members that the fisheries association of British Columbia made a submission to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects in which it was stated that commercial fishing represented the fourth largest primary industry in British

Columbia, and that it employed directly some 18,000 individuals, and indirectly, some 75,000.
One of the most important features of this bill is that clause regarding the control of the pollution of waters. This is becoming a very pressing problem. I do not intend to go into it in detail as I am sure there will be much said in this regard when the bill is before the committee for consideration. Generally speaking, what has been suggested is that the Fisheries Act be made to conform with the bill of rights.
I would like to ask the minister whether he has considered that penalties in regard to violations be set by regulation so as to permit adjustment upward and downward. Since 1932 the penalty provided was so low companies did not even change their methods of disposing of wastes. These companies felt they could afford to pay the penalty and continue discharging poisonous and toxic matters into the streams. The penalty as now proposed will certainly make this an undesirable course to continue.
We have listened to a great many references to international waters and the establishment of a 12 mile limit. It has been estab-listed by international arrangement, between the United States and Canada, that the waters lying from the south end of the Alaskan Panhandle, which divides the waters known as the Dixon entrance, south to the Queen Charlotte islands, and south again to Vancouver island, and the waters between those islands known as Hecate straits, to the mainland, are Canadian.
Foreign vessels do, however, operate in these waters. If at this time we were to declare the territorial waters lying between headland to headland, our jurisdiction in this regard is not being exercised. I realize that questions of reciprocal favours in regard to our fisheries may exist but if foreign vessels are to be allowed to fish in these waters it should be by sufferance and not by right. They should be allowed to do so perhaps by permission granted each year so that the permission can be withdrawn if it is in the national interest to do so.
One other problem has been puzzling me which the minister can perhaps consider. That is, how will the department prevent vessels in waters such as the straits of Georgia from jettisoning oil waste material into these waters? I might mention that in British Columbia we have a water pollution act which exercises a certain amount of control. It was brought into being because of the fact that the Fisheries Act, as it read, did not exercise control because of its inadequacy. There is a proposal in this bill to change that, and it will perhaps provide some control over

vessels operating in inland waters and prevent the discharge of waste material. I will reserve any further comment in this regard until we come to a detailed clause by clause consideration of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking on the second reading of this bill I do not intend to traverse the ground that has already been covered by my colleagues from Newfoundland. Suffice it to say that I agree thoroughly with the observations they have made about this bill. I must say I cannot refrain from making a brief comment-and a very brief comment, because I do not think it deserves much more-about the very laboured attempts of the Minister of Justice, using United States precedents, to show that he was introducing freedom, United States style, into Canada and in doing so justifying police methods which most people who supported the bill of rights thought were going to be ended by the bill of rights. I think perhaps until we get into committee that is all his speech merits by way of reply.
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse)-he was in the house until just a moment ago and I wish he was here-I see he is here, but not in his accustomed place-[DOT] had something to say which I think merited more serious attention than the observations of the Minister of Justice. The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg who is, I am sure, just as anxious as everyone else who represents a fishing riding to have the fisheries of Canada adequately protected, was disturbed lest unilateral action by Canada, if it should be taken, would provoke retaliation from the United States. Well, I must say I regard that as a sensible concern, and I think every Canadian ought to regard as a sensible concern anything which might endanger our market for fish in the United States which is absolutely essential to the well-being of the fisheries. I certainly agree with the hon. member about that; but I felt it rather strange that the hon. member should have waited until May 2, 1961, to express this concern because he had a wonderful opportunity to do it in June of 1957. I happen to have in my hand a clipping from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. of June 4, 1957, which reports the peregrinations of the hon. gentleman's leader through Nova Scotia, and in this report I read:
During his day-long tour, with scheduled stops at Chester,-
A place familiar to the hon. gentleman.
-western Shore, Mahone Bay, Lunenburg and Liverpool, Mr. Diefenbaker criticized the federal government-
That was the Liberal government.
-for not making a stand regarding laws which allow United States draggers to fish within three
Fisheries Act
miles of the Canadian coast while Canadian draggers have to respect a 12 mile limit off their own coast. He said that the federal government apparently was afraid of annoying the United States, although "if the United States was interfered with they would immediately make their stand known."
I assume the hon. gentleman was under the wing of his leader on that occasion, but there is nothing in the Halifax Chronicle-Heraid that I can find to show that the hon. gentleman expressed his apprehension about the views that his leader was expressing at that time, apparently for the purpose of getting votes for the hon. gentleman. It seems to me that that would have been the time to express this fear, that would have been the time to point out to the Prime Minister that he did not really know what he was talking about, that he was going to lose the market for our fish by threatening the United States in this way.
Well, sir, I do not believe in threatening the United States; I do not believe in any of this nonsensical business of trying to appeal to the public in the way in which the Minister of Finance used to do when he was over here. "We will speak in no uncertain terms". We all know the way he whimpers in Washington now compared with the way he used to talk. But I do say, sir, that I do not believe that, having gone through what we have gone through in the interval between 1957 and 1961, there can possibly be any real danger of any such retaliation for this reason.
We have had the conference on the law of the sea at which the present government put forward the views that were outlined by the previous government, views on which both Canadian governments agreed, and I am glad they did agree because I think the position we put forward was in our national interest and it was a good thing that all Canadians should have agreed on that. We very nearly got everybody else to substantially agree on that at Geneva. With one amendment which, if we did act unilaterally, we would want to make as a condition of our action, we did secure agreement and got the co-sponsorship of the United States. If it becomes necessary to act unilaterally, I would not advocate for one moment that we should do so without prior consultation not only with the United States, but consultation with all those other powers, particularly those that are interested in fishing in the north Atlantic who were willing to agree to the convention on the law of the sea.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you might call it five o'clock.

On clause 1-Incorporation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

Mr. Chairman,
when this bill was last discussed, which I think was some two weeks ago, we had another excellent contribution by the hon. member for Vancouver South. Once again he demonstrated not only his considerable knowledge of this particular subject but also his courage in standing up to what has been certainly very severe criticism in maintaining the stand that he has taken throughout this whole debate, a stand which I believe should recommend itself to many more of the party which the hon. gentleman represents. I was very glad to see the hon. gentleman take this stand, Mr. Chairman. Unfortunately, examples of courage of this kind are not seen too often, and certainly the hon. member must be made of pretty good stuff to stick to his guns the way in which he has.
We see quite a difference between his actions, for example, and those of another hon. member of his party who did differ on one vote and then disappeared when the matter was finally dealt with in the house. This criticism of the hon. member has gone on not only in the house but outside of the house as well. There is an article by Mr. Raymond Rodgers, who writes the Ottawa letter in the April 1, 1961 issue of Saturday Night. He has some comments to make on
TMr. Pickersgill.]
this situation and believes that some middle course should be struck on matters of this kind. This writer feels that some compromise could be reached between bloc voting and party anarchy.
This bill appears in many respects to be completely contrary to the announced policy of this government, of many of the cabinet ministers and even the Prime Minister. It is rather strange, therefore, to find only the hon. member for Vancouver South who seems to really believe this policy expounded by his leader and the other members of the cabinet. Certainly he has been the only one who has demonstrated during this particular debate that he believes what he says and that he really stands by what he says. One or two other hon. members have expressed some doubt about the matter, but that is as far as they were prepared to go.
I feel it is very important that we in this committee bend every effort to try to reverse the alarming trend toward more and more United States control of the Canadian economy. We have seen it in many fields, and we see it now extending into the natural gas and oil industries. I feel, and the rest of the members of this group feel, it is high time some steps were taken by this parliament to recognize this trend and to reverse it. We see a situation in which present company treasuries are becoming the instruments for extending United States monopolistic control over so many of our industries.
I hasten to say, Mr. Chairman, that I am not anti-American. I certainly do not believe the hon. member for Vancouver South is anti-American. Two members of my family have become citizens of the United States. I have many relatives and many friends in the United States. I should like to state categorically that I am not anti-American. However, I am anti-American-control of Canada's destiny. I feel that Canada's destiny and Canada's industries should be controlled by people in this country who would have at heart first and uppermost the interests of this country. I do not blame the people of the United States for doing what they are doing in our economy. They would be silly if they did not. If our Canadian government is crazy enough to hand over our country on a silver platter to the United States industrialists, they would be crazy enough not to accept it.
As I mentioned before, the Prime Minister and many of our cabinet ministers have, on different occasions, made clear and strong statements condemning the former Liberal government for allowing this to happen. Things were going to change. Unfortunately, we did not see too much change and certainly the bill that is before us now represents no

change at all. This is another of the many unfortunate things we have seen in the past, and the bill is going to permit almost complete United States control of another industry. This has been the policy for the last 20 years, but certainly it has been accelerated as the years have gone by. We hear lots of fine talk, and then after the talk is finished we see a bill like this presented. Only one member of the government is prepared to stand up and fight for the very things for which the government professed to stand.
At the moment, Mr. Chairman, over one-half of our manufacturing industry is controlled from outside the country, mostly from the United States. Over three quarters of our mining industry is controlled from outside the country, again mostly from the United States. The bill which is before us is going to open one more loophole which will enable United States control to be exercised over our oil industry. This means that many of the decisions which are of vital importance to the Canadian people are going to be made by people who do not live in the country and whose allegiance and interests are not necessarily those of the Canadian people.
It could be argued, as has been done on many occasions here, that we need United States investment in Canada. We need United States investment for Canadian development. This could be true to a certain extent, but what we do not realize is that most of this so-called United States investment does not come from the United States at all. In studying the issue for 1959 of U.S. Business Investment in Foreign Countries, which is issued by the United States department of commerce, we find that less than 20 per cent of the money invested by United States companies in Canada actually came from the United States. This means that over 80 per cent of the so-called United States investment in Canadian industry has actually grown up right in this country. It represents income generated in Canada by industries controlled by people living outside of Canada. This money represents undistributed profits, depletion allowances, depreciation, all United States controlled and allowed to accumulate in Canada because of the softness of our tax laws. These tax laws are much softer than those of the United States which relate to the same situation. This, of course, is one of the reasons these investors are so eager to get over here.
What this points to is that we are now permitting the Americans to buy us out with our own money. Certainly this is something that should be of vital concern to all hon. members in this chamber. This is a trend that is going to have to be reversed. This is one of the reasons that you so often see

growing up in this country a kind of anti-Americanism which is not really based on facts at all. It is not realized just what the true facts are. In the Atlantic, the issue of May, 1961, I find the Atlantic report on Canada. It has some interesting things to say about this feeling that is growing up in Canada. It states:
During the last months of the Eisenhower administration, signs of a critical deterioration in Cana-dian-American relations were everywhere apparent in Canada. Canadians were simply in a mood to be unimpressed by anything attached to an American label, from the Bomarc missile misfires to the U-2 incident, the uproar over Cuba, and the curtailment of U.S. spending abroad. Yet this cultivated contrariness had almost nothing to do with the political complexion of the American administration. The greatest boom the country had ever seen was grinding slowly into a recession of major importance and the Canadians were taking out their frustrations on the suppliers of the capital-American industry.
Then it goes on to say this:
That "American" is a dirty word in Canada cannot be denied. But it is used completely without animus or rancor, in the sense that "Colorado" is used with potato beetles, "Spanish" is used with influenza, and "German" is used with measles. In Canada, "American" only means where the problem comes from and it means no more than that. The problem itself is the end product of a series of economic developments of the last ten years. Like an instalment-plan addict without sales resistance, Canada has lived on cloud nine for the better part of that period. It borrowed frantically to finance its development. Then it borrowed to pay interest on its foreign debt. It sold off its resources and it mortgaged its future.
I might add this, Mr. Chairman. That appears to me to be a much better assessment of the situation in Canada than we often see in United States publications. However, I think this bill before the committee today is one very good sign of where this trouble lies and where it is developing. I think this has been pointed out clearly by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I also note again today that neither of the co-sponsors of this bill appears to be in the chamber. In spite of the eloquent plea of the hon. member for Vancouver South the last time we debated this bill, apparently we are still not going to receive any answers to the pointed questions he asked with regard to this bill.
In view of the oft-stated policy of this government and in view of the situation and the problems I have outlined here today, I cannot see how, in all conscience, hon. members of the House of Commons can give this bill passage until these questions are answered. I do not know why we cannot receive any answers today. I do not know whether the sponsors-I refer to the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Winnipeg South-have lost all interest in this bill. Possibly, if the answers were

supplied to these questions that were asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South, hon. members would be of a different mind.
One of the sponsors is here.

I am glad to see that the hon. member is back again. Since he is back I wonder whether he is prepared to answer the questions that were asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South when this bill was debated a few weeks ago.

They have been answered. I think the hon. member for Vancouver South would agree to that statement. It would not change his position on the bill but I think he was satisfied with the answers I gave him and put on the record.

The hon. member for Vancouver South has demonstrated many times in the past that he is quite able to speak for himself, and I have not observed him to rise in his place and admit to the fact that he is satisfied with any answers he has received. In fact, the last time I heard him speak here he was complaining bitterly because answers had not been given. I recall full well that he said the other day that the answers had been given when he was away. Certainly, those questions have not been answered to my satisfaction, regardless of whether or not they have been answered to the satisfaction of the hon. member for Vancouver South. Until those questions are answered, I certainly do not see how hon. members sitting on the government side can salve their conscience in passing a bill like this one in view of the policy that has been so often stated on behalf of their party.

However, because the hon. member for Vancouver South has expressed a difference of opinion-apparently his opinion differs from that held by other members on the government side-he has been accused in some circles-I think, wrongly and unfairly-of breaking party lines.
On a point of order. The hon. member for Vancouver South is not under discussion today. It is Bill No. S-2.

I am not discussing the hon. member for Vancouver South. I would not presume to do that in any circumstances. If we look at page 3765 of Hansard when Aurora Pipe Lines was under discussion on another day, namely April 18, we shall see some words spoken by the hon. member for Vancouver South right at the bottom of that page. In the last paragraph on that page, and then continuing over, the hon. member says:
I am not going to labour the points which have been pressed in this committee before with regard to capitalization stretching into millions to build half a mile of pipe line. The testimony in regard to this particular phase of the operation has been gone over in this committee time and time again. But it would be well for hon. members to read the testimony given to the standing committee and try to find out exactly what is being attempted. If they do I think there will be more of them come around to my way of thinking. The chief government whip has said that this is a private member's bill and hon. members are free to vote for or against it as they so choose to do. That is true.
I am relating my observations to those remarks which I have just quoted and to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South on an earlier occasion when he dealt with this same question of party control and whether people were free to vote for or against this particular bill. I am dealing with Aurora Pipe Lines in the light of the relationship between the ownership of the pipe lines company and the announced policy of this particular government in office, should this particular measure obtain the approval of parliament. I am dealing with the effect of that ownership upon our economy. This is where my remarks will lead.
As I said, I think the hon. member for Vancouver South has been unfairly charged with having crossed party lines. In my opinion he is the only member on the government side who really agrees with the Tory

policy; it is the other hon. members on his side of the chamber who have crossed the party line and who are in disagreement with the announced policy of this government as set forth in the speech from the throne in two separate places and as announced on a number of occasions by ministers of the crown who have spoken in this chamber to the effect that they intend to do everything possible to ensure a greater degree of Canadian ownership and control of industry in Canada. That is the party line, and the hon. member for Vancouver South agrees with it. But every one of his colleagues obviously disagrees with it if they support this particular bill, because the effect of the establishment of this company by virtue of this bill, having in mind the international financial relationships which exist between Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company, the parent company, and the United States-controlled Continental Oil Company will be greatly to strengthen the interests of another country in the development and use of a basic Canadian raw material.
In view of the internal financial relationship existing between the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company and the United States controlled Continental Oil Company it is apparent that someone on the government side deviated from the concepts contained in the speech from the throne. I do not say this with any intent to derogate the speech from the throne or His Excellency, but do so in view of comments made by government members both in this chamber and outside, in regard to the fact that it is desirable for this country to develop Canadian ownership and control of our natural resources. In this regard I commend the hon. member for Vancouver South who apparently is the only hon. member holding true to the concepts therein contained.
We could go into discussions regarding the interpretation of the National Energy Board Act, but this has been done often in the past. I would suggest that it should be uppermost in our minds in order to protect the development of our national resources in favour of Canadian industry, economy and workmen, to curtail, as far as we possibly can, ownership falling in the hands of interests other than Canadian. This subject has also been discussed on many previous occasions, and information in this regard has been placed on the record by many hon. members, with the exception of hon. members belonging to the Liberal party who have not done so because of the tenderness that exists there in regard to pipe lines.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Once bitten, twice shy.

Information in regard to the ownership and control of this company has been brought to our attention. Canadian national ownership is something that should be kept in mind during any discussions we may have regarding bills of this type. I do not think it is in keeping with the best sense of direction in respect of the ownership and control of our industries and resources to authorize this particular company to become established with a capital and share structure as is now proposed, because it will be contrary to our voiced concepts in this regard. I suggest companies that are established by virtue of the passing of private bills in this house should have share structures enabling them to discharge their duties with the best possible result to Canadian people and Canadian economy, and should not be allowed to be in a position where, because of outside ownership, their primary concern is the serving of interests in another nation.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South, the co-sponsor of this bill, and perhaps the sponsor in lieu of the hon. member for Bow River, has placed quite a bit of information on the record which is contained in a letter I understand was addressed to him. This information appears at page 3766 of Hansard for April 18, 1961. This information was provided in answer, at least in part, to some of the questions asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South with respect to ownership of the company itself.
This information shows that on December 31, 1960 Canadian ownership of the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited was 2.96 per cent. This was apparently an increase in ownership from 1957. The increase in total shareholdings was the difference between 306,000 and 525,000. The 2.96 per cent represents an increase of approximately 75 per cent in ownership of shares held in Canada since 1957. When one considers that 67.77 per cent of the shares are held by the Continental Oil Company, controlled in the United States, the 2.96 per cent is a drop in the bucket, and quite inconsequential. I would suggest that the increase in the number of shares held by Canadians, which has taken place over this three year period, is also inconsequential.
A further letter addressed to the hon. member for Bow River was read into the record and appears at page 3428 of Hansard for March 28, 1961. It also dealt with the question of Canadian ownership. It is suggested in that letter that it is desirable that Canadian ownership in the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited be increased. This suggestion is then qualified by the statement that the officials would like to see this increase take place. Because this has been a

Private Bills
concern of the hon. members of this committee for some time I would suggest it is natural for those officials to make such a statement. There were further statements made but perhaps I should not trust my memory in this regard. I will read from the letter as it appears on page 3428 for March 28, 1961:
At the present moment the company does not have any need for additional equity capital to finance its operations and accordingly, cannot make any definite prediction as to the timing or possibility of a further issue of treasury shares which could be offered to the Canadian public. However, we believe the past actions of the company in making a distribution of a portion of its capital stock back in 1957 before there was any strong public clamour for such action is the best possible kind of indication of the company's attitude and thinking on this subject.
While it may be outwardly desirable on the part of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company to have this percentage of ownership by Canadians increased, I wonder what is the attitude of Continental Oil Company toward relinquishing its 67.77 per cent ownership? The desire of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company is expressed in the letter, and it may be taken at its face value. Its desire, it says, is to have more Canadian participation in ownership but, according to the letter, this can only come from the issuance of additional shares from the treasury. This means that the percentage of Canadian ownership will not bear the same relationship as it does now.
If for argument's sake, they issue a certain number of treasury shares, then Canadians will have to buy in the same ratio as they now hold in order to maintain the same percentage of ownership in the particular company. If the amount of stock issued is increased and if the value of the stock increases because of activities on the stock exchange resulting in the turnover of shares-and the value of the stock could easily change the other way; but even if all this should happen-what about Continental Oil Company's 67.77 per cent ownership?
Is Continental Oil Company going to issue the shares that it already owns? Is it going to relinquish its 67.77 per cent control over Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company? Is it going to put on the market the shares that it holds? Is it going to sell them on the Canadian market through the Toronto stock exchange or some other exchange in order that Canadians may have the opportunity of purchasing them at whatever the going price may happen to be at that particular moment?
This is an important question. If it were not analysed from this point of view it may lead some people to believe that within 10, 15 or 20 years we may expect Canadians to have not 2.96 per cent ownership but 3.96

per cent, or 4.96 per cent ownership in Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company. But, without the action of Continental Oil Company, which has the controlling interest, in so far as offering or selling shares that it now holds is concerned, regardless of the number of Canadian shareholders, Continental Oil Company of the United States will still have the controlling interest in Aurora Pipe Lines through Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company. By that means, the ownership of the industry exploiting these resources will still, psychologically if for no other reason, be serving the interests of Continental Oil Company of the United States rather than the interests of the Canadian people.
These are questions which I think we must keep uppermost in our minds when considering whether this particular bill should be passed, or whether any changes can be made in it by the committee itself. I do not know whether it can, or whether it is desirable that it should. But I say that if we look at this from the principle established in the debate or by the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver South who I think did a commendable service for this country and the committee by taking the attitude he has and by using the approach he has, if we look at it from this point of view, from the point of view of serving Canadian interests and developing Canadian resources and owning an industry in Canada so that it serves the interests of the Canadian economy and the Canadian people we will be much better off in considering this bill than if we degenerate into-and I am guilty of this myself at times- lowering our sights and talking about relatively inconsequential differences of opinion as to what the national energy board should do or what the Alberta gas conservation board may do, has done, or will do.
This is the approach we must keep in mind. We must keep our sights on this particular question. I think if all hon. members will do that they will, as the hon. member for Vancouver South said-I think I can dig out his words very quickly as they appear on page 3765 of Hansard of April 18:
If they do I think there will he more of them come around to my way of thinking.
This is what the hon. member for Vancouver South said. I am not using my own words. I would not advocate that hon. members on the government side come around to my way of thinking because I know what the immediate reaction would be. The hon. member for Vancouver South used this approach and made his appeal from the point of view of Canadianism, from the point of view of announcements in the speech from the throne and from the point of view of his own party's

public pronouncements. Perhaps they should do what I am attempting to do now, even though on some occasions I may have gone a little overboard in niggling differences of opinion about side issues.
The hon. member can relax; it is six o'clock.
