speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. MacLean (Queens) for the second reading of Bill No. C-86, to amend the Fisheries Act.

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned this debate at five o'clock I was dealing with the fears that had been expressed by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse) to the effect that if we undertook to establish a 12 mile jurisdiction over the fisheries contiguous to our coast the United States might retaliate. I said that this was a legitimate consideration which we should take very seriously. I reminded the hon. gentleman that his leader, in peregrinating through the hon. member's riding in 1957, had promised to talk tough to the United States about this. At that time the hon. member, so far as the record shows, expressed none of the fears, none of the apprehension, that he expressed today. I suggest that perhaps that would have been the right time to do it.
Why didn't you do it?

Why didn't I do it? I was
not campaigning to put a Conservative government into office in this country. I was not trying to do anything to deceive the people of this country, either.
Mr. Pallet!: Not at that time.

Nor at any other time.
Why is it so important that there should be jurisdiction for the government of Canada over the fisheries out to the 12 mile limit? I think the best reason is the very reason 90205-6-268J
Fisheries Act
given by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg when he explained to us why it was that Canadian trawlers were kept by Canadian legislation 12 miles out from the Canadian mainland provinces on the Atlantic coast. It is very important, not only to give a reasonable opportunity to the trawler fisheries but also to give proper protection to the inshore fisheries.
I was rather astonished that the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg should have said, as he did this afternoon, that the inshore fisheries did not seem to matter very much any more. I am afraid the hon. member would find it difficult to obtain much support for that view. I have here in my hand an extract from the Chronicle-Herald of Halifax for Saturday, April 29, three days ago. The article contains a report of a speech made by Dr. Henri Fougere, who is on the staff of the fisheries technological station at Halifax. In the course of his speech, as reported here, Dr. Fougere pointed out that as recently as 1959 the inshore fishery accounted for 78 per cent of the cod landed in the Atlantic provinces. This means that the inshore fishery is extremely important.
As long as we are going to consider, sir, that under international law we have to allow foreign draggers to come within three miles of our shore it is no longer tolerable to keep Canadians 12 miles away from the coast of Nova Scotia. It is an indefensible position. It has been an indefensible position for some time. The only reason it has been allowed to continue-I am not blaming the government for this-is that the government has sought a solution of this problem by international means which would give the government jurisdiction over all trawlers, both foreign and domestic. I do not believe it would be reasonable to keep all trawlers out beyond the 12 mile limit everywhere along the coast. I do not think it would be reasonable, but I am not an expert. However, in those areas in which there is a flourishing inshore fishery, it is a shocking thing to have gear torn up by draggers, either foreign or domestic. This is the situation, and the inshore fishery is being ruined by these draggers.
If we had jurisdiction domestically, if we Canadians could decide where and under what circumstances fishing could take place, then there is no doubt but that we would be able to reach some reasonable modus vivendi with those countries such as the United States, Portugal, Spain and France which historically have fished in these waters, and perhaps even some of the newer countries, for a 10-year period of phasing out such as was defined by the proposal the United States co-sponsored. I would think,

Fisheries Act
sir, there should be support for the suggestion which was made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) a year ago to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) and to which the Leader of the Opposition referred again this afternoon, that we should seek agreement among the 54 nations that voted with us and the United States for our joint resolution. We should do so quickly, and should not dawdle about. Having reached an agreement with them, then we should do what many another country has done successfully, Iceland being the most recent example, and make a unilateral declaration that we consider our fisheries jurisdiction extends out to the 12 miles, and that we are going to endeavour to enforce it.
If we cannot get agreement among the 54 nations, then we should go to the half dozen nations that do fish in the northwest Atlantic to see if we can get a reasonable understanding among them, as the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) suggested a few moments ago. If that is not possible then surely if the 150,000 people living away up on the edge of the Arctic circle in Iceland can assert their sovereignty against the majesty of the Britannic crown surely a great country like Canada is not going to be afraid to protect what is our patrimony, what is our birthright, and what brought our ancestors to this country in the first place, the fishery of the new world.
I cannot believe, sir, that the United States government, which co-sponsored the proposal in Geneva, would repudiate that action. I grant that the United States has had historic rights. I am one of those who believe that we should always seek understanding with the Americans. I do not believe in making idle threats or in talking in no uncertain terms. I think there is a great deal more to be said for talking about these matters in certain terms, in moderate and calm tones and in sweet reasonableness wherever possible. In the free world today it seems to me that we have so many things in common and are faced with such great hazards that I would not feel that determined, reasonable and quiet negotiators would have any great difficulty in reaching agreement with the United States about this matter.
Why did you not do it before 1956?

The hon. gentleman, I think, asked why we did not do it before 1956. We started on a course in 1956, as my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition pointed out this afternoon. We started in 1956 on a course which has been followed precisely by the present government. Indeed, we
EMr. Pickersgill.]
had an example-and perhaps I have been provoked into saying this by the hon. gentleman-of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), at the very opening day of the session a year ago, producing this little booklet on the law of the sea and distributing it to all of us, so confident was the hon. gentleman that he was going to be able to accomplish what the Leader of the Opposition had started when he was in office. It was perhaps a little like the Columbia river matter. Perhaps hon. gentlemen anticipated their success a little before it had arrived. In any event, they were taking the absolutely essential first step. Obviously, the right thing to do is to get international agreement, if possible. I commend the government for following that course. I commend them for the zeal and vigour with which they acted at Geneva. The only thing I cannot commend them for is that they did not succeed.
I am not blaming them for that. I just say that I cannot commend them for it because they did not succeed. We all regret that fact but we must face it. This is a matter really of life or death to the oldest industry in Canada, the first of all our industries. It seems to me that it needs to be pursued with a good deal more vigour than that with which it has been pursued in the last year since the failure at Geneva.

I wish to speak very briefly on one of the principles-for that is what it is-in the bill now before us and so defined by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) who led off in opposition in the debate on this item earlier today. I refer to the item dealing with the 12 mile limit and the three mile limit.
Hon. members who were in the chamber this afternoon may now recall that during his remarks I asked the hon. member for Skeena, who had recommended unilateral action to enforce the 12 mile limit, how he would propose to enforce this 12 mile limit. I am glad to see that the hon. gentleman has remained in his seat throughout the debate because the issue of enforcement has been neatly avoided, in my opinion, by hon. members who have spoken here this afternoon. Indeed, the Leader of the Opposition-a man who has experience in international diplomacy and who knows that much more than fishing is involved in the breadth of the territorial sea-said that, in his opinion, I had chosen a very poor symbol when I inquired about enforcement.
For example, I asked what the hon. gentleman would do if a Russian trawler sought to enter the sea. The Leader of the Opposition said that the hon. member for Halifax -if I am paraphrasing him correctly-is apparently not aware that the Russian area is 12 miles. I do not like to disappoint the Leader of the Opposition. In the field of international affairs there are vast areas of knowledge which are not in my possession. However, it just happens that I did know that fact. Indeed, I think I knew a little bit more about it than the Leader of the Opposition put on record as his knowledge today. There appears to be confusion in the house when we speak about territorial limits and fishing rights limits. The position of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is identical wth that which it commenced in Czarist days. Since 1909 the Soviet union observed a 12 mile territorial area.

The Soviet union had not come into existence then.
Fisheries Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I said earlier that the Soviet union had followed the same principle as that initiated by the Czarists in 1909. This was to define an area of 12 miles as the territorial sea.
Hon. gentlemen who are provoked or inspired by today's debate could consult the publication of the Society of Comparative Legislation and International Law available in the library of parliament. It was consulted earlier in this debate by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten). I have no doubt that other hon. gentlemen have seen it. It gives a synoptic table of national claims to the breadth of the international sea and the territorial sea. Therein they will find, as the hon. member for Humber-St. George's listed today, claims varying from three miles to two hundred miles. But this was not the Canadian position. If I understand the matter aright-and in responsible representation of my constituents I hope I understand it aright, and I have thought that I did so-at the Geneva conference the Canadian position was that we should like to see enshrined a three mile territorial sea.
Six.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will desist from interrupting me I will presently come to the full story. I quite accept the proposition that it was ultimately resolved at six miles, but I should like to tell my own tale about this. The position taken originally by the Canadian delegation was for a three mile territorial sea, but with an additional nine miles in which the coastal state would have exclusive fishing rights.
We already have rights, some of them extending beyond three miles, for other activities of government. I think we claim customs jurisdiction out to nine miles. It may be that my recollection is correct and we have customs jurisdiction out to nine miles. Various nations have claimed jurisdiction for sanitation, fiscal policy, immigration, the breadth of the territorial sea and fishing areas.
The original Canadian position at Geneva was for a three mile territorial sea and a nine mile exclusive fishing area. The United States' position was not this at all. The compromise position was a six mile territorial sea and a six mile additional sea, which the Canadian delegation would have accepted for exclusive fishing rights, but the United States' position would have confined this to a nonexclusive fishing zone wherein would be granted the so-called traditional rights in perpetuity.
Indeed, this was carefully explained to the house on July 25, 1958, by the then minister

Fisheries Act
of northern affairs and national resources. I will cite what the minister is reported as having said as reported at page 2683 of Hansard of the House of Commons for that date:
-in the final analysis the central issue before the conference was not whether there should be a fishing zone but whether it should be subject to existing traditional rights as proposed by the United States or whether it should be exclusive and without impediment as proposed by Canada.
So in respect of the area of territorial sea Canada has not laid claim to a 12 mile area. Yet today, if I paraphrase the remarks of hon. members correctly-and I seek to do so-we heard the hon. member for Skeena recommending unilateral action. The hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Tucker) said, if I heard him correctly, that all that was required was courage to go out to 12 miles.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) was more modest and said that we ought to seek some understanding with the 54 nations who voted with us.
I said nothing about territorial limits.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is quite right; the hon. gentleman did not say anything about territorial limits. I accept that. I did not identify him or any hon. member as being individually confusing and confused about this matter. I am simply saying that in the debate this afternoon, and I can become more vigorous about this-
Please do.
Go ahead.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
-hon. members talked about unilateral action towards the development of a 12 mile limit but desisted from saying how it would be enforced.
It is all very well to say that all that is lacking is courage. It does not take any courage to be a braggadocio. It often takes courage to be reasonable and to take reasonable steps. I am sure the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate will forgo in patience the reading of his newspaper to hear the reiteration of that sweet word describing a characteristic which he so often himself admonishes us to manifest. Reasonableness may be a more sure and courageous ground than what is described as courage. In the press of other business it is easily forgotten that at Geneva we did not have the support of the United Kingdom, the United States of America- which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate says we should now seek to obtain- nor did we have the concurrence of China, France or the U.S.S.R. Indeed, I believe that was the first occasion upon which a simple

majority had been carried over the objection and negative vote of five permanent members of the United Nations security council.
The question that I asked this afternoon still begs an answer. How would we enforce a 12 mile limit? The hon. member for Humber-St. George's has referred to a Batin American nation which lays claim to a 200 mile limit. At the time the hon. member looked at me quizzically because I was shaking my head, by which I intended to convey to him the impression that he surely did not mean to suggest that this was a valid or enforceable territorial sea. It is violated, if one may use that phrase; it is certainly entered, traversed and countertraversed many times every day because other nations do not accept it as the territorial limit.
But they declared it as such.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
They have declared it as such. The hon. gentleman and his colleagues, if I understand them aright, would have us declare a 12 mile limit for Canada but they will not answer the question of how to enforce it. What purpose is served by legislating for domestics and nationals a law which cannot be enforced?
This afternoon I used the example of a Russian trawler. I do not wish to pursue that because in other matters affecting marine life and the conduct of other fishery in the high seas we are making, and we hope we will continue to make, good progress with Russian negotiators. We are all responsible here, even private members, not to exacerbate international relations which are apparently progressing to the good service of our people.
With regard to the Icelandic experiment in which Iceland declared a 12 mile limit, I was interested in the interpretation put upon this by several hon. gentlemen this afternoon. They said this proved that you could enforce a 12 mile limit. With all respect to their opinion, the Icelandic situation has appealed to me more as a case which proved, not that you can get agreement but that you almost cannot get agreement.
Is there anyone in the house, least of all the Leader of the Opposition, who will say that dealing with the government of the United Kingdom, which has a tradition of fair play reasonableness and justice running back centuries, if you are Icelandic, is like dealing with the U.S.S.R.? If it is, it has not been apparent in years of negotiation to which all of us have been witness.
I conclude by drawing the attention of the hon. gentleman to the convention on the territorial sea and contiguous zone which was arrived at in Geneva. Article 14, says in part:

Subject to the provisions of these articles ships of all states whether coastal or not shall enjoy the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea.
Thereafter it says:
Passage of foreign fishing vessels shall not be considered innocent if they do not observe such laws and regulations as the coastal state may make and publish in order to prevent such vessels from Ashing in the territorial sea.
That is very clear. It defines the innocent passage of a fishing vessel for the purpose of our debate. But the territorial sea in Canada extends for three miles, and the most we ever tried to achieve was six miles, not 12. As to the additional six miles, we came to no effective result because of a divergence between the position taken by Canada that the additional miles should be reserved exclusively for our nationals and the United States' contention that regard should be paid to the traditional rights in perpetuity of other fishing nationals. The convention says:
The coastal state may take the necessary steps within its territorial sea to prevent passage which is not innocent.
Then, further on:
The term "high seas" means all parts of the seas that are not included in the territorial sea or in the internal waters of a state. The high seas being open to all nations, no state may validly purport to subject any part of them to its sovereignty.
The burden of what I wish to say is this. The anomalous situation which has prevailed since 1952-and I wish to arouse no partisan disaffection with regard to this matter-has, of course, given rise to criticism. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said correctly that the proper course to have taken was to have sought international agreement. The position I take is that this is still the correct course of action, and that the use of the term "unilateral action" is-and this is the harshest word I shall speak tonight, for want of a better-grandstanding. Here is a situation which presents a great anomaly. Foreign vessels are fishing up to three miles of the Canadian coasts while Canadians are required by statute-by the Fisheries Act enacted under a previous administration- not to come within 12 miles for the purpose of fishing, and this is the situation which has been left until now for amendment by the present government. Canadians are required by statute to stay out to a limit of 12 miles.
Hon. gentlemen opposite know that this angers, irritates and arouses Canadian fishermen. What do they offer as a solution? The grandstand technique of saying that Canada could and should unilaterally move out to 12 miles. Well, the test of that is whether it can be enforced.

Are we enforcing the three mile limit?
Fisheries Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We are enforcing the three mile limit because it is internationally accepted.
We are not enforcing the three mile limit. All you are talking is nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
All my talking is not nonsense, but we shall leave that to other judges. The internationally agreed territorial limit has been three miles, and hon. gentlemen well know that. We are enforcing the three mile limit upon other nationals. What 1 am trying to say is this. If you say that unilateral action to 12 miles is a desirable course, how do you propose to enforce it? Would you enshrine in statute form a law which could not be enforced? To limit the breadth of the territorial sea, important as that is to our fisheries, is not solely confined in its significance to that industry. It has important defence repercussions, and hon. gentlemen well know, or should well know, that the U.S.S.R. at Geneva let it be known in informal talks that it would stand firm on a 12 mile territorial sea because there are things which cannot be done in a 12 mile territorial curtain of sea that can be done between 12 miles and three miles off the coast.
Earlier today I put a question to the hon. member for Skeena. We shall come to this matter again when we consider section 55 of the Fisheries Act and the amendments thereto. I asked the hon. member: how do you propose to enforce this? If a Russian trawler or another foreign trawler did come within 12 miles, what would you do? How would you be prepared to enforce it?
What do you do inside the three mile limit?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We enforce the Canadian domestic law upon those who are proper subjects of Canadian law, that is, upon nationals of Canada.
Do you not enforce it on foreign boats?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We enforce the three mile limit because it is generally accepted internationally.
You will have to tell it to somebody else.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I may have to tell it to somebody else. The point is that we are not discussing the three mile limit now. We are discussing a 12 mile limit. The solution put forward by hon. gentlemen opposite is to go out to 12 miles but nowhere in this grandstand play has one of them proffered a definite assertion that the opposition, if it had the responsibility, would take the responsibility for enforcing the statute should

Fisheries Act
some other national come in and call our bluff. The proof that the opposition would not do it resides in the fact which was simply and correctly stated by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
If hon. members who sit with him will read his remarks tomorrow they will discover that he has pulled the rug from under them. He said quite properly that the opposition, when they formed the government, had sought an international agreement. They had the opportunity then to go to 12 miles and the action they took is generally known. It is no use at all telling our fishermen we can enforce a 12 mile limit unless we mean to enforce it, and this cannot be done unless we are prepared to go to the extremities of enforcement.
Have we not enforced it on our own people?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is always a matter of perplexity to me to understand what transpires in the hon. gentleman's mental apparatus.
That is mutual.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I may say this to the hon. gentleman. During his remarks, when I asked him a question he very discourteously told me that I could make a speech later on. I should like to be able to make that speech, if the hon. member does not mind. However, if he wishes to engage in a debate there will be one winner and one loser.
It would be widely acceptable to my fishermen if we could get out to 12 miles. But how do you get out there? How do you enforce it? Would you ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) to send Royal Canadian Navy forces to fire shots across the bows of foreign vessels? The United Kingdom did this in the waters off Iceland. Are we prepared to do it? What I am suggesting is that the unilateral action which was recommended here, except by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, is not the right solution.

I am sure the hon. gentleman is not consciously seeking to misrepresent what I said. He has repeated that statement two or three times but it does not happen to be a fact. I said if we could not secure any kind of international agreement we should make a unilateral declaration, and I stand by that statement. I would prefer that the hon. gentleman would not go on, by repetition, appearing to create the impression that I said something different. I think that all other courses should be taken first.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I did not intentionally try to misrepresent the hon. gentleman. Today he made one of his few lucid speeches, but it

is usually difficult not to misrepresent him. I agree that he said every course should be explored but, in saying that, he did not agree with his fellow hon. members. The other hon. members wanted unilateral action. The hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Tucker) said all that was needed to go out to the 12 mile limit was courage. If that hon. gentleman really meant that, let us see him get behind a gun shield and enforce it, because if he does not mean to enforce it, it would not be good law and should not appear on the statute books.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. gentleman, before he, in a manner of speaking, takes his seat, would permit me to ask him one question? The hon. gentleman talks about grandstand plays. Would the hon. gentleman say whether, when his leader was travelling around Nova Scotia promising that if he got into office he would establish the 12 mile limit, he described that as a grandstand play and asked the right hon. gentleman how he was going to enforce it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not in the habit of defending the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) against a man who was born in Winnipeg and now sits in a Newfoundland seat in respect of which he has not even had a nominating convention.
Mr. Speaker, I was not born in Winnipeg.
Lucky old Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must inform the house that if the hon. minister speaks now he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to review for a few moments some of the contributions that have been made to the debate this afternoon. Before doing so I would like to point out that as far as the action in respect of amending the Fisheries Act is concerned, we have seen over the last year and a half to perhaps two years, a classic example of an age old gambit indulged in by the opposition. This is perfectly within their rights so to do. I have no objection to those members of the opposition doing so at all. The tactic is, of course, to try to pressure a minister, by repeated questions and suggestions from time to time, into making premature statements with regard to government intentions, or ill conceived statements on government policy so that if, because of events which subsequently transpire, the government is not able to make good in regard to the statements the opposition will be in a position to belabour them.

I have been asked time and again what we intended to do about amending section 55 of the Fisheries Act which, in certain areas of Canada, the maritime provinces, requires large Canadian trawlers to stay 12 miles from our shores. Intermingled with this question have been a great many questions about the law of the sea, a subject which is actually entirely different. Hon. members are out of order in discussing it on this particular bill, although it is closely related. I have no apology to make when I say that it has been my habit, perhaps partly from training, and partly by nature, to be rather reticent when questions of this sort have been put to me in the past.
The second move open to the opposition is an attempt to guess what government intentions are. Having satisfied themselves that they have guessed, members of the opposition then announce as their own policy what they think the government is about to do and, therefore, try to claim credit for it. This is all strictly within the rules but is, of course, a strategy as old as oppositions are. I am not finding fault with these tactics at all but I would not want those members of the opposition to think they have discovered some new tactic in this regard. I hope they have not deceived themselves into thinking they have succeeded in creating the illusion that they thought of these tactics first, and that they forced the government into panicky action practically against its will, because nothing could be further from the fact.
A number of hon. members expressed the opinion this afternoon that the government was panicked into suddenly taking action to amend the Fisheries Act because a private bill was introduced on March 22. I do not want to detract in any way from the initiative of the hon. member who introduced that bill. However, I would not like to let him or anyone else in the opposition think that these were the facts of the matter, that this proposed bill to amend the Fisheries Act was thrown together in panic by the government.
I should like to assure you, Mr. Speaker, and all hon. members, that these amendments are put forward now as a result of long study, the accumulation of knowledge with regard to the deficiencies of the present act, and as a result of complaints that have been made on the one hand by individuals of the public who felt they had been discriminated against and, on the other hand, by the staff of this department which has from time to time reported that, because of the way in which the act was drawn enforcement was from time to time frustrated.
The Leader of the Opposition cited, as proof of the theory presented, the fact that this bill was not mentioned in the speech from the throne. I think it is common knowledge that 90205-6-269
Fisheries Act
a government is not obliged to mention, in the speech from the throne, each and every bit of legislation which it proposes to introduce in a session of parliament. The fact that this bill was not mentioned therein does not in fact prove anything. I find this exercise on the part of the members of the opposition quite amusing because of my familiarity with it, having sat in the opposition perhaps longer than most of the hon. members now there. As I have said, these are not new tactics at all. I would suggest, however, with the passage of years the present members of the opposition may develop more skill in this regard so it will not look so obvious.
Methinks the lady-or in this instance the laddie-doth protest too much.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do want to say that I welcome the implied support for this bill because, after all, imitation is perhaps the greatest means of flattery. I am sincerely appreciative of the fact that most hon. members, regardless of where they sit in this house, although they have naturally had certain reservations and criticisms, generally conceded that this was a step in the right direction. It may be grudging support, but nevertheless I accept whatever measure of support they see fit to give the bill.
I hesitate to say this because I fear it might sound condescending but I do not mean it in that sense at all. I was in opposition for quite a while. This business of trying to guess what the government is going to do and then jumping on the bandwagon is quite a fine tactic if it is executed with finesse, but in doing this an opposition member is in danger, when he jumps on the bandwagon, of reducing himself to the status of the fly in the Aesop fable who sat upon the axle tree of the chariot wheel and said, "What a dust I do raise". I certainly would not want that to happen to any of my hon. friends in the opposition, but I think we should look at what are the facts of the matter.
Last year on the estimates, when the question was raised of amending the Fisheries Act with regard to the insufficiency of penalties for permitting the pollution of waters to occur-I believe this was raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) -I said that this was under careful examination with the idea of bringing the act up to date in that regard. Then the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) raised the question whether the bill of rights when passed would be in conflict with the Fisheries Act. I remember I told him on that occasion that since the bill of rights had not passed this was a hypothetical question and therefore I had nothing further to say except it was the

Fisheries Act
concern of my department to see that there was no conflict in the legislation which I had the responsibility of administering. There were other questions. I was asked by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse), I believe, whether section 55 of the Fisheries Act would be amended, and I answered him on that occasion by saying that the problem was being studied even then, and further back than that, which is the fact.
We come now to March 22 of this year when the private bill was introduced. Hon. members suggest that this was what prompted the government suddenly to introduce this amendment to the Fisheries Act. I should like to point out that on March 14, eight days before the bill was introduced, I had this to say in the house with regard to amendments to the act, as reported at page 2963 of Hansard:
I am hopeful that it will be introduced. We have been working on suitable amendments to the Fisheries Act for several months and I am hopeful that we shall have a bill to bring before this session of parliament.
As I said, I have been reticent about making flat statements as to what is going to happen in the future. I think it cannot be said that this was something that was thought of after March 22, when I said on March 14, as reported in Hansard that we had been working on this very amendment for many months. I do not intend to belabour the point, but I want to clear up the situation and give credit where credit is due, namely to the officials of my department who are concerned, as I am myself, with protecting the resources of the sea and making sure that those renewable resources are protected so that those engaged in the fisheries will in perpetuity have the opportunity to win their livelihood from those resources of the sea.
Various members devoted a great deal of time to the question of territorial waters. As I have said, strictly speaking, I think this question is out of order so far as this particular measure is concerned and I do not wish to impose on the house but I should like briefly to say that the question of the law of the sea affects many departments of government. Besides the Department of Fisheries, it affects customs, transport, defence and many others. Therefore, these various interests are brought together in the Department of External Affairs in dealing with other countries. Because the law of the sea is an international problem therefore it is the responsibility of the Department of External Affairs.
I should like to mention at this point that an excellent job was done through external affairs by the Canadian delegation at the two

conferences on the law of the sea in Geneva. We almost won success; we just missed it by one vote.
A great deal has been said about the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his actions during previous election campaigns in saying that we will stand up to the United States and see to it that the rights of Canadian fishermen are protected out to 12 miles. I should like to point out that this government has gone about this problem in a logical way. We made an attempt to seek international agreement on the widening of the territorial limits and an exclusive fishing zone contiguous to it, and gained a great measure of support from the nations of the world in this regard and had the success of eventually having the United States come to common ground with us as far as this problem is concerned.
As I said, this is the responsibility of the Department of External Affairs and I do not presume to speak for that department, but I can say that the government is continuing to address itself to this problem with undiminished zeal. The fact that the anomalous situation which has existed for years has increased in severity under changing conditions because of section 55 of the Fisheries Act has no direct connection with the wider problem. The fact that this anomaly is now being removed by this measure does not indicate in any way that the other problem is hopeless, or that there will be any diminished effort to gain international agreement with regard to a wider territorial limit and/or a contiguous, exclusive fishing zone.
This particular problem of our own larger trawlers not having the same privileges as foreign trawlers in certain areas is a domestic problem which is being rectified by our own legislation, as it should be. The fact that this is being done does not imply, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) seemed to think, there has been no progress in the field of achieving agreement in the wider field of international affairs.
A great many members suggested that the thing for us to do was to take unilateral action. The Leader of the Opposition and some other members seemed to think that the situation had now got to the point where this was the only course left open to the government. That is not the case. I want to assure the house that no avenue will be left unexplored, no stone unturned, in order to secure action which will result in greater benefits for Canadian fishermen in the waters adjacent to our own coasts.
However, this matter of just declaring unilaterally that we are widening our territorial waters or exclusive fishing zone, is not as simple as that. We have to be able to establish sovereignty if we choose to follow that

course. This is not something that is easily accomplished it other nations do not accept the stand taken by Canada. I think there is still good hope of international agreement being achieved in this field, at least among a major group of nations.
The Leader of the Opposition deplored the fact that there was no amendment to this act to declare unilaterally we were widening our territorial waters. I should like to point out that this act is concerned only with the regulation of the fisheries. I should like also to add that the act of parliament which gives the government power to declare what are and what are not our territorial waters for fishing is the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. The government has power under that act, if it deems wise so to do, to declare certain waters to be territorial waters for the purposes of fishing without any further legislative action. If the government proposed to declare a zone for exclusive fishing rights, that might be a different situation and might require some legislation or amendment to the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act.
I do not intend to say anything more on this subject because, Mr. Speaker, I feel that strictly speaking I have been out of order for the last 10 minutes or more. I think Your Honour, in fairness, would not call me to order since other members who preceded me have been given considerable latitude in connection with this matter.
Several hon. members expressed some doubt about the wisdom of the right of seizure of fishing equipment by fisheries officers. At least one hon. member said that it was not at all reasonable that fisheries officers could seize equipment and then the minister be under no obligation to return it for 90 days if no legal proceedings were taken in the meantime. I should like to point out that at the present time there is no time limit. I believe that everyone will agree that a limit of 90 days is an improvement over no limit at all.
I should like to point out further that this 90 days is the maximum in practice. If equipment is seized, legal proceedings are taken as quickly as possible. If and when this amendment to the act is passed, it will be for the courts to decide whether or not the equipment is forfeited. I think this will be a great improvement on the present act under which the minister and the fisheries officers have very wide arbitrary powers so far as the seizure and forfeiture of equipment is concerned.
The fact remains, however, it is necessary under some circumstances to seize gear, especially gear that is illegally set. If it is left alone, it continues to take part in the breaking of the law. If it is not seized, the 90205-6-269i
Fisheries Act
law will continue to be broken until the person responsible comes back to recover not only his gear but his illegally caught fish after the fisheries officer has gone. In many cases, this equipment is part of the evidence and it is impossible to convict without it.
I want to add, though, that the law is designed to protect the vast majority of Canadian citizens who are law abiding. I am convinced this act will place no hardship on them. It is directed against people who are breaking the law. I might say that ignorance of the law is no defence. The purpose of the seizure of equipment is to protect the law abiding fisherman and the resources upon which he depends for a livelihood so that his efforts to earn an honest living will not be sabotaged by those who would, for their own quick gain, destroy the resources on which the majority of the people depend. I am proud to add that the vast majority of fishermen agree with this point of view. They insist on strict enforcement of the law when they see it being flagrantly broken by someone who has no regard for it.
I might say, too, that this power of seizure does not necessarily mean forfeiture. Whether or not the equipment is to be forfeited will be decided by the courts. If it is forfeited, that may be part of the penalty or the court may order the equipment returned. In this way, as one hon. member expressed it, the punishment will fit the crime. That is not the case at the moment. In many cases now equipment is seized but the court does not order that it be returned nor does the court order that it be forfeited. Often the guilty person is fined. In some cases the fine is small and is imposed in anticipation of the fact that the equipment that has been seized will be forfeited by order of the minister. The party who was found guilty of an offence then appeals to the minister for the return of his boat, truck or whatever it happens to be. He cites the small fine which was imposed as an indication that the infraction was regarded as a minor one and, therefore, he should not suffer this additional punishment. These matters will now be considered by the courts and if forfeiture is ordered, it will be ordered only as part of a larger penalty or it may be the whole punishment.
I think it goes without saying that it is not the purpose of this act or of the Department of Fisheries to make life difficult for those who try to abide by the law. If the law is broken inadvertently on occasion we try to temper justice with mercy, so to speak. I think the situation is as fair as it is possible to make it.
There is little I want to add, Mr. Speaker, except to say that many of the amendments

Fisheries Act
which we now propose to this act are introduced so that no penalty will be suffered by anyone until a determination has been made as to whether or not he is guilty of any infraction of the Fisheries Act or the existing regulations by the due process of law.
In that way we hope that the interests of innocent parties will be protected to a greater degree than they have ever been protected before. These amendments are not perfection but I am convinced that they are a vast improvement on the Fisheries Act as it now exists and has existed for a great many years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?
Question.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1-"Fishing vessel".

Mr. Chairman, it is usual for a minister, when winding up the debate on his bill, to spend the greater part of his time replying to criticisms that have been made on second reading. This evening the minister occupied at least one third of his time, I would think, in trying to refute an argument, which was put forward not by me but by some of my colleagues, that this bill had been hastened because of another bill which I had introduced some time earlier this session. I made no such claim and I do not think it is important enough to spend all that time upon it. However, from the fact that the minister took so much time in trying to disprove this point, when added to what the Minister of Justice said earlier today, it seems that we have touched a sensitive point. As my colleague the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate pointed out in his quotation from Shakespeare, "Me-thinks the lady"-or laddie-"doth protest too much".
We have certainly had a great deal of protesting here today. We have had much more protesting about this matter than we have had argument. A clever man once said that if you throw a stone in the dark and a howl comes back, you know that you hit something. It seems as though my colleagues happened to hit something here.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Later I will answer any question the hon. member wants to put to me.
Does that remark apply to boomerangs?

It is not important who thought of this first. I can put on the record the fact that I had made a draft bill three years ago. Then we had the bill of rights. However, there is no point in doing this. The important thing is that this bill is before the House of Commons today and I am happy, and I expressed my delight. Whether it speeded anything up or whether it had no effect at all, certainly the fishermen are going to benefit by the fact that this bill is before us much sooner than we had a right to expect either from the speech from the throne or from the list of legislation which the Prime Minister gave us only a few days ago.
My chief reason for taking the floor is to reply to some of the arguments made this evening by the hon. member for Halifax. I do not know how we are to distinguish him from his colleague. I think perhaps we can do it by calling him the shorter member from Halifax. The hon. member is a fine example of a person who, if he does not succeed in convincing anyone else either by his logic or his oratory, leaves no doubt that he himself is thoroughly convinced. This evening it seemed that he was carried away by the exuberance of his oratory and talked himself into a bit of a trance.
The hon. gentleman made a great deal of the question of enforcement. I dealt with that point of enforcement this afternoon. I said that in my province we did not have the means of enforcing even the three mile limit and that we were not able to enforce it this winter. I have case upon case which I can cite in order to prove that statement. I put one case on the record when I cited the Spanish trawler by the name of the Santa Amalia which violated the three mile limit and destroyed the gear of our fishermen.
We cannot enforce the three mile limit with the small ships we have. I made that point quite clear. I said that we wanted not only ships that were five times larger than the ones we have now but that we wanted five times as many of them. This is an example of the talking in circles that was performed by the hon. member for Halifax this afternoon. He took the position that it was impossible to enforce a 12 mile limit. Just a few minutes ago the minister told us, as he told us yesterday-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I was not in the
chair when the discussion on second reading started, but the minister has raised the point that it was out of order to discuss this question of the 12 mile limit. Before the debate continues on that line, I should like to hear what the hon. member who has the floor or any other hon. member has to say on this point. If the changing of the three mile

limit would involve an amendment to an act other than the Fisheries Act, it seems to me that the point made earlier by the minister would be well taken. Even if this matter was discussed on second reading, the hon. member will realize that a discussion on clause 1 of a bill in committee is not necessarily the occasion on which to continue the debate which has been closed.

On the point of order may I say this. I feel that I should have the right to reply to arguments that have been made in this chamber this evening by an hon. member. That is all I am seeking to do. I would call to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the fact that I have not mentioned territorial waters. I have used the term "12 mile limit". I do that for a purpose. It is a phrase that is meaningful to the fishermen in my constituency. When we say "12 mile limit" we are not splitting hairs about whether it is territorial water. We are mainly concerned with the fishery and the protection of fishing rights. Whether you call them jurisdictional waters, an area of jurisdiction, or zone of fishery rights is immaterial. As far as we are concerned, it is a zone of water in which the fishermen's rights to fish are protected. If you wish me to be technical I will refer to it as a zone of fishing rights; but that is all I mean by the phrase.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have to be technical, as the hon. member realizes, because we are studying the bill clause by clause. If the hon. member agrees with what the minister has said, that to extend the three mile limit for territorial waters, or fishing rights to 12 miles would necessarily require an amendment to another act, he will agree with me that it is out of order to discuss it now.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, I have the right to reply to argument that has been made in the house this evening by another member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I have indicated to the hon. member, the debate on second reading has been closed. We have to be relevant in committee in discussing the bill clause by clause.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may make an observation since you invited observations from other hon. members on the point.
I think it has been the custom of the house, and a custom that was frequently reiterated and almost codified by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, particularly when he sat on this side of the house -though I have not heard him argue so strongly for it from the other side of the house-that a brief general discussion on the
Fisheries Act
first clause of a bill, the kind of argument that arose in the debate on the principle of the bill, has always been permitted. Not extended speeches, but a brief discussion has been allowed.
I think it would probably save the time of the committee, considering that the debate was largely concentrated on this particular point, if the one or two hon. members who wish to clarify one or two points in this connection were allowed to proceed, as has seemed to be customary. speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I may say a word on the point of order, I think that even those who are quite skilled in international law and various other aspects of this matter may find it difficult to arrive at a line of demarcation between the amendments proposed here and the larger problem of the law of the sea.
In view of the fact that such a wide range was allowed in the former debate, I suggest that perhaps there would be no great objection if some latitude were given in this regard. I think it might expedite discussion of this bill, rather than prolong it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Very well, as long as I am relieved of any responsibility.
We will be tolerant, sir.

The hon. member for Halifax belaboured the point over and over again, how are you going to enforce a 12 mile limit? We have been enforcing a 12 mile limit on Canadian nationals and there is a clause in this very bill which is going to remove that 12 mile limit for Canadian nationals. Surely there is no difference as far as the means of enforcing a 12 mile limit is concerned. The means of enforcing it in respect of one ship will also be the means of enforcing it for another.
This is done by ships, the same as is done in the case of a three mile limit. It is the same thing. The means will be the same, but you will need more facilities to carry out the enforcement. You will need more ships, more patrols. You will probably need naval ships and air patrols. But the machinery and methods that work in the case of Canadian ships will certainly do the same job in the case of foreign vessels.
The hon. member cited the experience in Peru. Has the hon. member forgotten that even though Peru has extended her area of jurisdiction 200 miles out to sea, it is not so very long ago that she confiscated three whaling ships belonging to another power-I think

Fisheries Act
they were under Greek registry-and took them into her home ports. That is what we would have to do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I just draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that I did not mention Peru at all. It is pretty obvious that he was not paying any attention to my remarks. I do not know where he gets his information from, but I said nothing about Peru.
The record will show.

I am pretty sure I heard the hon. member mention Peru, and I will look at the record tomorrow. However, we do not have to rely on Peru. We have the example of a little nation like Iceland. We have the example of a small nation like Norway, which is smaller than Canada. Norway has found some way of doing it.
Surely, if little countries like Iceland and Norway can enforce a 12 mile limit, what logic is there in saying that Canada cannot do the same?
It may be all right for my hon. friend; he may not have many constituents who are suffering because of the encroachment of foreign draggers. But I can assure the hon. member that last winter foreign draggers did affect not only Newfoundland fishing ships but mainland fishing vessels that were operating out of Port aux Basques.
I should like to tell the committee what happened in this case and I will quote one or two excerpts from a telegram I received from Mr. T. J. Hardy of Channel, Port aux Basques. This gentleman sent me a telegram on behalf of the fishermen of that area.
For the information of hon. friends I may say that Mr. Hardy is one of the most enterprising fish operators in my province. He is a man who owns and operates a fish plant. If one of his skippers becomes sick, he can get aboard that dragger, take her out and set his gear the same as any skilled fisherman; and he can build his own ship and fit her out. That is the kind of man we have in Newfoundland, and he knows what he is talking about.
This is what happened. The fishing in this area was good-

How many copies of that
speech are you going to send out?

-and the fishermen were bringing in catches of 150,000 pounds of fish a day. The foreign draggers came, and the catch fell from 150,000 pounds a day to 20,000 pounds a day. It does not take much imagination to realize what effect that has on the livelihood of these fishermen.
Read the telegram.

Not only were our people
deprived of their livelihood, but the fish that were being caught were largely wasted. The fishermen were not able to handle the catch on board these foreign ships; the weather was cold; it was freezing a little and too fast for them to handle the fish. They had to throw the catch away, or it was washed away. There were so many dead fish floating around in this area that it was possible for people who worked in the offices there to pick up, after office hours, 1,500 pounds of fish per person. That is the sort of thing that is happening.
This was wealth of which my constituents were deprived and it was wealth that was being wasted. It was not doing anybody any good. This sort of thing goes on over and over again, year after year. My hon. friend thinks we should be satisfied to let that situation continue indefinitely. We are not going to let it continue indefinitely. We are getting pretty well fed up with it. It is all right to be sweet and reasonable, but how long can you be sweet and reasonable when your family is starving and when your livelihood is being taken away from you?
The answer to that situation is this. I think the hon. member himself put on the record this afternoon that at the Geneva convention 54 nations were in agreement on a six mile territorial limit plus a six mile zone of fishing rights. If those 54 nations were sincere in reaching that agreement, what is there to prevent them from getting together themselves and making that agreement work? How long should one remain sweet and reasonable while all those 54 nations who agreed to it in principle and supported it in Geneva and worked out a solution delay in putting it into effect?
What would you do?
I say we have been pussyfooting long enough. The time is coming when we must stop pussyfooting, and if it means taking unilateral action, I say we should take it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Perhaps I can make a few brief remarks. I was not in the chamber when the hon. gentleman said that for the purpose of definition he would call me the smaller member for Halifax-
The shorter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Perhaps I could refer to that. Heretofore, Halifax, which is an anomalous constituency resembling that of the hon. Minister of Fisheries inasmuch as it is represented by two members, used to have what was described by hon. members as a senior and a junior member. I always thought this was somewhat pompous and I must say I would be delighted if the hon. gentleman cares to distinguish between my colleague and

I by referring to the longer and to the shorter hon. member for Halifax. I can tell the hon. gentleman that it is in no way offensive. The best things in the world come in the smallest packages.
That is a reflection on your colleague.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It is not a reflection on my colleague at all. It is simply an assertion that we do not have a senior and junior member in Halifax as used to be the case.
I do not wish to prolong this discussion, but, frankly, I think the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo is a great deal more convincing when he is talking the language of lake Couchiching or Mackinac island, than when he is talking about taking unilateral action. Moral ReArmament comes much stronger from him than these statements that we should go it alone and do this and that. Certainly reasonableness should be the language of M.R.A. rather than talk of unilateral action. It is gratuitous of the hon. member to say that I am not concerned. I am concerned. We are all concerned. I am concerned about the Newfoundland fishery because I am a Canadian and because I am a member of parliament. I have said nothing here which should have aroused the hon. gentleman's vigour or acerbity in any way. I simply ask whether those who recommend unilateral action are prepared to enforce its consequences.
Hon. members opposite say that we can now enforce the three mile limit. The answer is very simple. It is elementary. We have jurisdiction under Canadian law over the nationals of Canada both in Canada and abroad but we have no jurisdiction over the nationals of another state. What would hon. members opposite advise doing if nationals of another state came inside the 12 mile limit? Is the hon. gentleman prepared to get into a boat and fire the first gun? That is the question he has not answered.

The answer is very simple. We would do exactly the same as we would do if they came inside the three mile limit, and if the hon. gentleman was not so dense he would know. The chief duty of any nation and of any government is to defend its nationals and to protect their livelihood. That is our duty here. The livelihood of our people is at stake and it is being jeopardized by nationals of some countries who themselves claim or at least try to claim a 12 mile jurisdiction. The hon. gentleman has spoken as though the three mile limit were something sacred, something handed down from Mount Sinai. It was only the range of an old time cannon. That is all the three mile limit was, and then a number of nations agreed on it. Well, we have
Fisheries Act
outgrown the three mile limit. We have outgrown the cannon. We are out in space now. We are orbiting around the world. The cannon with the three mile range is out of date and we have to bring ourselves in line with events.

I intend to be very brief. I made my contribution this afternoon. However, I must make a comment or two about some of the observations made by one of the hon. members from Halifax. I shall be very careful how I refer to him because I was in the kindergarten group that he lectured a little while ago when he climbed onto Mount Olympus and looked down on us from a great height.
Despite the fact that the hon. member spent some time talking about the 12 mile limit, only two things seem to emerge. One was that he seemed to think that any extension of sovereign power beyond the three mile limit would be an act of aggression against, I presume, the rest of the world. The other point was expressed by his repeated question, how would we enforce it? The hon. member inferred that any attempt to extend our rights to 12 miles would automatically involve armed action. That was the inference, although it was not stated in so many words.
My own impression is that Canada, which has been active in negotiating the extension of territorial waters, could, if she negotiates long enough and hard enough, win by means of negotiation alone. The prospects are by no means hopeless. In any case I think our position would be so well established on moral grounds by general agreement that, helped out, perhaps, by a little of that braggadocio about which the hon. member talked, the 12-mile limit would become an accomplished fact.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We have just seen precisely in the last two minutes the contradiction of which I spoke in my remarks on second reading. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo said "Take unilateral action." The hon. member who has just sat down said "The situation is not hopeless; I believe in negotiation".
This is precisely the point. I did not say anything in my remarks against the 12 mile limit. My remarks were directed against unilateral action to try to secure it. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said he would resort to unilateral action only as a last resort, by which he meant he wants to have the best of both arguments. I say it is perfectly apparent that hon. members opposite are not prepared to enforce a 12 mile limit. It cannot be enforced. If a law cannot be enforced, it is not a good law, and if it is not good law it should not be on the statute books. I believe in negotiation. Now

Fisheries Act
that this matter has come out in free wheeling debate, I may say I was appalled to hear a former Nobel peace prize winner come into this house this afternoon and advise taking unilateral action. Negotiation is the only way to achieve a 12 mile limit. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate did not check his script with that of the Leader of the Opposition because they said opposite things. You have got to negotiate because you are not prepared to enforce it. If we can establish a six mile limit it will be better for our fishermen than a three mile limit. I am saying that I do not believe in unilateral action at this time. I do not believe the hon. gentlemen, who have said they do, are prepared to take the consequences in the way of enforcement. What could be clearer than that statement?
Since the hon. gentleman seems to know better what I said than I do myself-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is possible.

-perhaps I can put this in a way that even that hon. gentleman, who has neither the will nor perhaps the capacity to understand, will find it hard to misrepresent. My position is not necessarily that unilateral action be taken and that was precisely the position taken by my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition. I think that the people of this country will be rather more impressed by the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition as to what might be possible in international politics than they will by the shorter hon. member for Halifax. The fact of the matter is that they all know that a little country like Iceland, having made a unilateral declaration, has succeeded, as I pointed out earlier, in getting the majesty of Great Britain to accept it, reluctantly, and in some instances with some difficulty. I do not believe that we are such pusillanimous people, that we Canadians are so frightened by our own shadows that if we can get a convention, by agreement in advance with other countries concerned, we will not do so. I do not believe that if we set our hands to this task we will fail. In fact, I am quite confident that we occupy such a position in the world that we would be successful in doing this.
How long would it take?
The Conservatives will take too long.

If the members of the government are as much interested as the hon. member for Halifax in securing this, it will certainly take until after the next election,

and until my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition becomes prime minister.
That will take another 25 years.
When that happens it will not take very long, as it will not take very long to get this country moving again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened this evening to the debate since 7.45 and have found some of the remarks most interesting indeed, especially those made recently by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. I wrote some of them down. He said, we enforce the 12 mile limit on Canadian nationals and they obey the law. It is only natural that all east coast fishermen who are good Canadians would certainly obey the law. The hon. member went on to say, if we can enforce the 12 mile limit on Canadian fishermen we can enforce it on fishermen from other countries. He said it was easy to do this. He suggested that all we need is more patrol ships and more air patrols and that we, like Norway, could enforce a 12 mile limit on any ship operating off the east coast.
I believe tonight that the opposition has really gone on record in so far as the east coast fisheries are concerned. I do not believe that hon. members want to see large trawlers leaving Halifax, Lunenburg, Louisburg or St. John's, Newfoundland, under protection of gun boats supplied by the Royal Canadian Navy, and aircraft supplied by the Royal Canadian Air Force. If that is the position of the Liberal party, and I think it has been well stated, I am pleased to see that it has finally been placed on the record. I do not approve, as the member for one of the largest fishing ports on the north Atlantic coast, and I raise strong objection to the remarks put on the record by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
I believe this government realizes that it has a duty not only in respect of deep-sea fishermen, but inshore fishermen as well. I have both types resident in my riding and I recognize the value of inshore fishermen to the Canadian economy. It is evident that the Liberal party does not wish deep-sea fishermen to have equal chances, as do fishermen of other nations. Members of that party discussed the situation in such a way that they have led us to believe they want our fishermen kept 12 miles off the coast without the opportunity of enjoying the same rights as those fishermen of other nations. I think this is a wrong approach and would suggest, under this government, that there will be no second class citizens, no second class fishermen. We intend to protect their rights.

We have heard other statements made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate suggesting that I was not interested in inshore fishermen. In my riding of Queens-Lunenburg there are a large number of inshore fishermen, lobster fishermen, as well as ground fishermen, and I should like to go on record as stating that as long as I represent that riding I will endeavour to see that they receive a fair share of the harvest from the sea.
Clauses 1 to 13 inclusive, agreed to.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, May 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Churchill for the second reading of Bill No. C-77, to provide for the rehabilitation of agricultural lands and the development of rural areas in Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in support of Bill No. C-77, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for introducing this bill. I want to say at the outset that this is one of the most important pieces of legislation that have come before parliament this session. This bill is of great importance to the people of my riding and I personally feel that it will have the effect of raising the standard of living of many people in the area.
The interlake area is primarily an agricultural area and is composed mostly of mixed farming. In the Selkirk constituency we have some excellent land. We also have some marginal and some submarginal land. This legislation is designed to raise the standard of living of those engaged in agriculture and primarily of those on marginal land. I can see that this legislation has great possibilities of doing that for farmers in my constituency.
The interlake area has never been included in a P.F.R.A. district. The reason given for excluding it was that the P.F.R.A. was set up for drought areas and conditions in the interlake area were the opposite. No matter how you look at it, damage caused by soil being too wet or flooded is every bit as bad as or worse than damage caused by drought.
Under this legislation the interlake area will now receive the benefits that other areas have received under the P.F.R.A., and therefore this area will probably see more immediate benefits than many other sections. Farmers will now be eligible for assistance
Marginal Lands Development for dugouts and the greatest benefit will come from the establishment of community pastures.
This piece of legislation is bold and imaginative. It deserves the support of all the people of Canada. If this plan for rural development succeeds, and if the federal and provincial governments advance the money to make marginal farm rehabilitation successful, this legislation will have important social and economic results for agriculture and for Canada.
In the past the trend has been for farmers to move off the farms and when several leave the same district it makes that particular community poorer. If this legislation bolsters the income of marginal farmers and of other more successful small farmers as well, it can revitalize the whole rural scene and renew prosperity for small business in rural areas as well. It is important that this legislation be supported by provincial and municipal governments. It offers social and economic benefits to rural people, and it will stop the exodus of rural people to the large cities. It is important that local chambers of commerce, service clubs and other organizations render support to this rural rehabilitation and development program. If everybody digs in and gets behind this legislation it cannot help but succeed.
When the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) was speaking on the bill last night he adopted a rather negative attitude. He did admit that he was supporting the bill but nevertheless he found fault with the preamble. Actually, the preamble is an excellent one. It reads as follows:
Whereas agriculture in Canada is undergoing technological changes that necessitate adjustments on the part of many Canadians engaged in this basic industry in order to maintain or raise their standard of living;
And whereas all Canadians, and Canadians engaged in agriculture in particular, may benefit by projects providing for the alternative uses of agricultural lands that are marginal or of low productivity, by projects for the development of new opportunities for increased income and employment in rural agricultural areas and by projects for the development and conservation of the soil and water resources of Canada;
And whereas such projects can best be advanced on the part of Canada by the undertaking of research and the providing of assistance to provincial governments and agencies thereof with respect to such projects;-
From the preamble hon. members can see that the bill covers a very wide scope and deals with the alternative uses of land and rural development projects. It is true, as has been said in the debate previously, that some of those projects will not give immediate benefit. It will take time for them to show real benefits to the people.

Marginal Lands Development
I wish to make a passing reference to the remarks made last night by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). In speaking on this bill last night the hon. member referred to having lived in the bush of northern Manitoba. These remarks can be found at page 4186 of Hansard. This was the second time during this session that the hon. member referred to Ashern as being in the bush in northern Manitoba. The first reference may be found at page 3657 of Hansard. I am sure that the people of that town and the surrounding area do not appreciate being referred to in these terms, since this type of reference gives the impression that they are backward. This is directly opposite to the truth. The town of Ashern and the surrounding area are a very progressive community.
