speechtext: Having two cabinet ministers at the same time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
That is correct, but I do think that the hon. member himself has got bushed and is completely out of touch with the conditions in Manitoba. The people of this district are industrious and proud of the opportunity of being able to help themselves. Through their hard work and initiative they have prospered.
When speaking on this bill last night the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate went on to refer to being in the bush of northern Manitoba. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Jorgenson), interjected, as reported at page 4186 of Hansard:
In one of the areas that will benefit most by this bill.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said "no". This indicates that he has lost touch with Manitoba, or else he just does not understand the bill. It is true that the farmers in the area are growing oats, wheat, barley and some specialized crops. However, there is only one grain elevator located on the C.N.R. line north of Warren and that is at Moosehorn, nine miles north of Ashern. This does indicate that the area is not a heavy grain producing area. The main revenue for this district is derived from livestock and livestock products. There are four creameries located in the district at Lundar, Eriksdale, Ashern and Moosehorn. This area, being a heavy livestock area, will benefit greatly from this legislation. Farmers will now qualify for assistance for dugouts, stock water dams, irrigation, irrigation projects and the greatest benefit of all to this type of area can be community pastures.
Throughout the years the people of the interlake area requested to be included in the P.F.R.A. district but their requests fell on deaf ears. These requests were made through
[Mr. Stefanson.l

the rural municipal council, and the council of the rural municipality of Signes was one of those councils making a request. Anyone who looks at a map of the P.F.R.A. district can see that the interlake area sticks out like a sore thumb because it has been left out of the green area which is the P.F.R.A. area. I have a copy of the 1958-59 report for anyone to see.
These municipal councils have passed resolutions at their district and annual conventions requesting the federal government that their areas be included in the P.F.R.A. district. I am sure the people of that area of Manitoba will not forget the shabby treatment they received at the hands of the former government, a government of which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was a member. About a year after I was first elected I submitted this report to the government. At that time these people had given up hope of ever getting any action on this type of legislation. The report I submitted to the present government was received with sympathetic consideration and is now being implemented through this piece of legislation. The interlake area will now receive the benefits which it was previously denied, that is the benefits that are granted under P.F.R.A.
The hon. member also mentioned that he had been in that part of the interlake area in 1911. I came to that area a little later with my parents in 1915, and not to the town of Ashern because they settled in the district of Vestfold. The only difference is, however, that I have a far greater assocation with the district than the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate since I arrived there in 1915 and have lived there continuously except for eight years spent in Winnipeg. This particular piece of legislation will bestow many benefits upon the interlake area because it deals with alternative use of land. We have many small farmers in that area who are located on a quarter section of land which is not good farmland. I am sure that in time, through the instrumentality of this measure, these people will be relocated.
The people of the area will receive a great deal of benefit as a result of the establishment of community pastures. I want to refer to the district where I first settled in 1915 with my parents. There were many settlers living in the district of Vestfold at that time. Today there are only a few farmers left. There have been great improvements made in the breed of cattle. In those days most of the farmers did not have good stock, but today you will find some of the finest cattle herds in Manitoba in that interlake area. A farmer by the name of Albert Thorgilson from Vestfold, Manitoba, exhibited two animals at the winter fair in Toronto last

fall. This indicates the type of stock being raised in the interlake area. In addition, a hog producer, Clarence Edwards, from Stonewall, for the past two years won an award for marketing the largest number of grade A hogs in the province of Manitoba. I believe he has marketed 90 per cent or better in grade A hogs, so you can see that the area produces quality hogs.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I just want to reiterate that I feel this bill deserves the support of all members in this house and the support of all the people throughout this great land of ours.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have not the slightest
desire to quarrel with the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson). We are very good friends, and I hope will remain so. I do think he misrepresented what I said last night, and I should like to correct him. When I went to Ashern in 1911 there was a good deal of bush. Even in 1915, when the hon. gentleman came to that part of the country, there was still a lot of bush. If the hon. gentleman had read on from the word "No" in the middle of page 4186 of Hansard for yesterday, he would see that I said this community would not need the benefits of this kind of legislation because of the progressive things that had been done by the people there. The hon. member mentioned those things in his speech, the wonderful cattle and the wonderful hogs being raised there. The people have done these things for themselves, and it was in seeking to praise that that I said what I said last night.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the minister on his appointment and I commend him for bringing down this legislation. Fifty years ago, Mr. Speaker, a man with a stout heart and a skeleton outfit could set himself up as a farmer with fairly good prospects of making a success. In other words, he could get a foothold on a quarter section of marginal type land and make a success. Time and the advent of mechanization have changed all this. Tractors and power machinery are very expensive. They require larger units of land for economic production and operation.
The operator of the family farm soon found himself in difficult circumstances, with rising costs barring the way to expansion, while retarded produce prices tended to limit and depress his standard of living to the point where the very existence of the traditional family size farm was seriously threatened. This was and is a problem all across the world. It is certainly not confined to Canada. Some countries surrendered to the trend and concentrated their agricultural operations in huge collective and corporate farms, while
Marginal Lands Development others instituted immense programs of subsidization, control of production and so on.
This government has committed itself to a different course of action. First, it believes that the independent family farm is the backbone of our economy as well as of our traditional democratic way of life. Second, Mr. Speaker-this is the point I want to stress- the government believes that the custody of our most precious natural resources, the productive topsoil of our arable areas, can most safely be entrusted to the care of family ownership where conservation and continuity of interest go hand in hand to preserve this heritage.
To qualify this statement a bit, may I say this. I mentioned the trend in different countries toward such things as collective or corporate farms. It stands to reason that management and workers on this type of operation would not have the down to earth feel of the soil. Their interest under pressure must be to take out as much as possible, without giving much thought to the preservation of the soil for future generations. Family ownership, on the other hand, can be entrusted from generation to generation to take care of the soil.
Mr. Speaker, I am reminded of an incident that happened to me on an Ontario farm when I was very small. One day in talking to me my grandfather picked some soil up in his hand and rubbed it a bit. He said to me, "Son, you be good to the soil and it will be good not only to you but to future generations". I think this is an important point. Years hence when we have exhausted our oil and mineral reserves, our top soil if properly protected will go on producing in perpetuity.
Third, this government believes that Canadian farmers, if given an opportunity, would be fully capable of reorganizing their industry into economic family units, each capable not only of producing a good livelihood for the operator and his family but of repaying long term credit.
These convictions led the government to set up, for instance, the Farm Credit Act which reflects a new concept of agricultural credit. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this measure has set up a creative process which should revitalize agriculture and do so on a self-liquidating basis. I think the fact that such a solution is possible is in itself a tribute to the basic soundness of Canadian agriculture and to the character of the Canadian farmer.
The previously mentioned legislation and other measures that have been brought down are only part of a major offensive. The Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act-I refer to Bill No. C-77-apart from

Marginal Lands Development working in certain specific areas of marginal and submarginal lands, will co-ordinate and make use of all these provisions previously mentioned in order to resolve the problems facing the agricultural industry today.
This legislation encompasses the widest participation and will enable the federal government to enter into agreements with the provincial government. The minister has stressed the fact that this participation must be started at the grass roots something which is the saving feature. In other words, it must start with a firm foundation and work up from the people themselves, rural and urban, through the municipal level to the senior governments. It is what I call a nationwide project. This measure provides our non farmers as well with an opportunity to take part in this national revolution. I should like to remind them that the health and welfare of our farming industry is fundamental to the health and welfare of our whole economy.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the future of Canada is not dependent upon the wealth and resources of the country but rather upon the character of its people. I submit that this legislation provides an opportunity for the expansion of a sound economy and, as well, the development of a strong character in our people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that, at the resolution stage, we, on this side of the house, have supported the principle of this bill. However, we supported it because the minister had given it a tremendous build up.
I am sorry that this legislation should come before the house at a time when the committee on agriculture and colonization is sitting, as was also the case last night. I also regret that the government whip saw fit, last night, to accuse us of not being present at committee sittings. As a matter of fact, as reported on page 4186 of Hansard he stated:
There is not a Liberal member down here.
Mr. Speaker, I find this statement quite strange, as he himself was present at the beginning of the sitting, and I want to rectify the gratuitous statement he made last night in the house.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, we did approve the principle of Bill C-77 with regard to the proper use of soil, and more particularly to the rehabilitation of agricultural lands and the development of rural areas in Canada.


As a matter of fact, we have been promoting this principle for a long time, because, if I am not mistaken, the Senate committee appointed by the former government went thoroughly into the matter.
We all know that farm revenue in some districts is inadequate; the minister stated so himself at the resolution stage, when he said that, in the province of Quebec, only 47 per cent of the farmers would benefit from this bill. Yet, when the resolution was discussed, the minister said he had great hopes of being able to consult the provinces as well as the farm organizations between the time the resolution was submitted and the discussion of the bill itself. That is what he said, as reported on pages 3263 and 3264 of Hansard:
Following the introduction of the resolution in January I thought there would be a debate for two days. Then I intended to go to each of the provinces, see the provincial governments, sit down with them and work out the general framework for a series of agreements that I thought we should work toward, especially the areas where research has to be done before agreements can be completed. Following that meeting with the provinces there will be a time lag, as they work on this, in some instances of three or four months. I want to discuss with them the terms of the bill to see if it is broad enough to cover the various types of agreements we have in mind. Second, I want to go to the farm organizations, who have been most co-operative and helpful over the years in suggesting this idea, show them the legislation and ask if they have any ideas for broadening it.
When the minister closes the discussion, I hope he will tell us whether he took these steps by getting in touch with the provinces and farm organizations.
Moreover, on March 23, 1961, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) made the following statement, which appears on page 3278 of Hansard:
Let me read to the committee the recommendation of the minister of agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan, Hon. I. C. Nollet-
Now, Mr. Speaker, comes the part of the recommendation quoted by the federal Minister of Agriculture:
1.	Provision of financial assistance in connection with agreed upon projects, on an approved basis.
2.	Making top level technical and professional advisors and consultants available, as requested by the province.
I wonder whether this bill includes a particular formula, as it seems to be rather general in scope.
Yesterday, in the absence of the Minister of Agriculture, it was his parliamentary secretary (Mr. Jorgenson) who introduced the bill. He stated among other things, as reported on page 4183 of Hansard for May 1:
The bill itself fits into the broad philosophy of this government in respect of agricultural policy.

The subjects of bills that have been introduced into this House of Commons and have been passed as legislation include the following: a program of price stabilization to alleviate the effects of the fluctuation of prices owing to economic conditions beyond the farmers' control; the introduction of a crop insurance program designed to minimize the effect of fluctuation in yields caused by weather conditions beyond the farmers' control.
I was quite surprised to hear the parliamentary secretary boast about the crop insurance act, as we all know that very few provinces have yet availed themselves of this scheme and that in fact, the scheme is being tried out in only one of the provinces, namely Saskatchewan.
The parliamentary secretary went on to say:
The bill outlines in three separate phases the intention of the government. First of all there are the projects for the alternative uses of land.
The minister has on several occasions indicated what he has in mind in this respect. He has outlined that many areas of Canada which are presently being used for agricultural purposes could be put to better use for the production of trees or as reforestation projects.
Here again, I think the act is too general and raises some doubts, because if you look at this year's estimates, you find that the Department of Forestry will spend $400,000 on reforestation. In future, will reforestation be carried out by the Department of Agriculture under this act, or will it be carried out by the Forestry Department? That is a question I should like the minister to clear up.
Furthermore, the parliamentary secretary, on page 4184 of Hansard, quoted yesterday from a report wherein it was stated that in any such plan, all levels of government, and I quote:
-will be involved and voluntary organizations such as chambers of commerce, agricultural societies, and community development corporations must lend their assistance to a co-ordinated program.
Therefore, it means that once again the government is counting on the co-operation of organizations for the implementation of this bill. It should not however be inferred from this statement that chambers of commerce and farm organizations have not done their share in the past to help the cause of the farmers.
I said the bill is unusually brief and that we are unable to detect any definite project in it.
In addition, I frankly admit that the statement of the parliamentary secretary caused us to wonder further when, as reported on page 4185 of Hansard, he said that this statement was taken from an item in the Canadian
Marginal Lands Development Federation of Agriculture news and information bulletin of January 1961 and entitled "A Rural Development Project in Quebec". This is what he said then:
There are many mountains and hills in that area-
He was addressing himself to the member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey).
-and some of the farms are of a marginal type. One young farmer, Real Boulanger, a confirmed skier, decided that the community had real potential as a skiing resort. He and his family and friends organized Mount Sutton, Inc. in February of 1960, and purchased 2,300 acres of land on the north side of Mount Sutton, the highest peak within 100 miles of Montreal. Then came the development of a first-class ski resort.
A little further, we read:
Jean Lessard, one of Canada's 1960 Olympic skiers, has agreed to provide skiing lessons. What has it meant to the community? Sutton is a rural community, and most of the local businesses were dependent upon the farm. The resort has brought new business. Twenty five people have been employed on the project, and it will provide fulltime employment for from 15 to 20 people all winter.
I say that this bill is too wide in scope, since everything seems to come under agriculture. We have reached the point where we are dealing with the development of ski clubs.
I wonder if indeed the object of this bill, and the purpose of the minister, is to promote such developments on submarginal farms.
And so, we can think up almost anything, or contemplate any project at all under a bill as vague as this one.
Moreover, as I was saying, this bill provides for no clear-cut project; it rather deals with such things as studies, researches and enquiries. Naturally we approve the principle of the bill, but it must not be limited to research, enquiry and study; it should also provide for projects that could be undertaken on submarginal farms.
This bill offers nothing in the way of definite projects with the result that, when it is passed it will be impossible for us to tell farmers on low yield land that such or such project may be undertaken on their farm. We were expecting something better and we feel that the bill could contain specific projects. Moreover we believe that if the bill is passed this year, the act could not be put into force immediately, since there is no provision for it in the estimates. It means that no subsidy will be paid this year unless we are requested to approve a supplementary vote.
During the debate last night, the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Ormiston), a government

Marginal Lands Development member, said the proposal would be very expensive. He surely meant that the government would be providing large amounts so as to make this legislation practicable. It is rather hard to assess the government's generosity because we still do not know what the program covered by this legislation will be.
There has been reference to conservation in western Canada and to development of marshlands in the maritimes. There again, it is nothing new since both items are in this year's estimates for agriculture.
Last night, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) referred to reforestation and forest products. As I said a few moments ago, we can well wonder whether the proposed new legislation, in the matter of reforestation, will be administered by the Department of Agriculture-which already had a similar division-or by the Department of Forestry.
As can be seen on page 4199 of Hansard, the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Danforth) said that the opposition is disturbed.
We certainly are not, because we feel there is really nothing here to disturb us. This legislation is too vague to enable us to discuss properly projects that might come out of it.
Mr. Speaker, we are relying on the Minister of Agriculture, and we shall find out after a while whether this bill will give the results which the minister promised at the resolution stage and promised previously in the build-up given this bill, which had inspired confidence among farm organizations of the province and throughout the country.
However, as I was saying, Mr. Speaker, we approve the principle of this bill.

speechtext:
At the outset I should like to voice my disapproval of a statement made last night by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) to be found at page 4188 of Hansard. It reads as follows:
This legislation is not going to contribute in any way at all to the solution of any of our immediate problems. Indeed, it may do the reverse unless we are very careful, because at the present time it would be a very grave error indeed to take anyone off a subsistence farm in order to consolidate holdings and make someone else's farm more efficient and put the person removed from his farm in the slums in one of our cities on relief.
I just want to say that provision is made in Bill No. C-77 for certain action to be taken which would refute that statement. I
do not know what the hon. member means by "immediate". I know it could be soon.
This bill has also as one of its objectives the arresting of migration from the land. The main part of the hon. member's statement implied that persons removed from farms by the application of this bill would go to the slums. That is a reflection on our rural people.
This legislation is unlimited in the benefits it can render to the whole nation, especially to rural life. This bill is of particular interest to me owing to the fact that agriculture is the largest industry in my riding. Therefore, I welcome the opportunity to support it.
Bill No. C-77 provides an incentive for constructive and visionary thinking. It creates an atmosphere of awareness of the vast scope of possibilities which can be useful in the improvement of farm income and the restoration of certain natural resources so vital to the accomplishment of the desired result.
This bill, with all its ramifications, when implemented in co-operation with provincial governments or agencies thereof should provide a wide field of diversification for rural people, and as a result many families will be able to maintain their way of life on their limited holdings.
In my constituency of Grey North and the surrounding areas we have some fine farms and progressive people. We also have many marginal and submarginal farms which do not make sound economic units. Many of these farms are being vacated and sold to holders or larger units. However, others on these farms, where they have perhaps spent their lives, as their parents before them did, are reluctant to leave. Anything that would supplement their income so that they could continue living on these locations would be acceptable. With these people in mind, I will make some suggestions which I think will be helpful.
The government could assist by soil testing and other research necessary to provide a sound basis for any of these operations.
Financial assistance will be a necessity in some of these fields of endeavour. I am thinking now of enterprises that could be satisfactorily adopted by family units. We have many areas suitable for blueberry production on which the Department of Agriculture has up to date information. Other low lying areas could be utilized for the

production of cranberries. Marked success has been achieved by several in this field. This could also be said about blueberry operations, especially in Newfoundland where this is a million dollar industry.
Game farming is relatively new and offers excellent possibilities. Pheasant and other game birds are raised to supply the ever increasing number of hunt clubs. A few others offer sportsmen the opportunity to hunt pheasant and other game birds on their farms on a per day or per bird basis. These birds are produced on the farm and released when stock on the preserve is in need of replenishment. Many more of these farms will be required to supply the thousands of sportsmen who would like to hunt where game is available.
While I am on the subject of catering to sportsmen, I would like to mention fish farming as another means of bolstering the rural income. We have thousands of sport fishermen searching the country for streams, ponds or lakes which might yield some reward for their hours of angling. Many farmers own excellent locations for the development of fish farms. I might add that thousands of fish farms are being operated profitably in the United States. We do have some such farms operating successfully which derive most of their revenue from supplying large hotels and restaurants with their requirements of speckled and rainbow trout. Many more people could be absorbed in this industry.
Fur farming has made a worth-while contribution to rural life in Canada over the past 50 or more years. However, expansion in the field of mink and fox production is not warranted at this time. We did, however, import over $71 million worth of Persian lamb skins last year. It is claimed that these can be produced profitably in Canada and could, of course be maintained on submarginal land during the pasturing season. This production would not create a meat problem as the lambs are killed shortly after birth.
We also imported in 1961 over $2 million worth of muskrats which could be produced on our own marshes and lakes. The provision in the bill for water conservation and resources management should remedy this situation and add substantially to rural income. Other fur imports to Canada in 1961 amounted to nearly $14 million. This is perturbing when one considers that we are traditionally a fur producing country.
Not far from my home in Grey North there lives an enterprising young man, Mr. Arnold Kuhl, who can rightfully claim to be the
Marginal Lands Development originator in Canada of a promising young industry known as "farm vacations". The idea has now spread to several provinces and each year more farmers will identify themselves with the enterprise and share and expand its possibilities. These farmers supply accommodation in their homes to urban families seeking an opportunity to enjoy rural life. This sort of holiday is becoming very popular because whole families can now enjoy a splendid vacation at reasonable rates in an environment that is healthful and appealing to children. Many farms through the country possess spacious homes which provide ideal circumstances for the promotion of farm vacations. Of course, these people are quick to provide other attractions, of which there is a large variety. Farm vacations open an avenue by which farm people may secure a larger share of the tourist dollar.
A sugar bush can be maintained on rough areas which are unfit for agriculture and, properly managed, can be the source of extra revenue to the family farm.
These sidelines which I have enumerated could be promoted on family units over a wide area of the country. Some of the projects would also lend themselves to specialization. I draw attention to them in the hope that provincial governments, or agencies thereof, through the provisions in this bill, might promote them among the rural people, 20 per cent of whom now operate farms that yield less than $1,200 a year to their operators.
It has been mentioned that marginal and submarginal farms could be converted to forest or tree farms. The Christmas tree farm is the only part of this program that would make a practical operation for individuals. Other reforestation of any magnitude is a long range program and would of necessity be the responsibility of large pulp and paper companies, the provincial and federal governments, or all three working together. This bill provides for such action, which should be one of the projects for immediate consideration and expansion.
Reforestation of large areas which have been timbered is taken care of to some extent by nature, but these areas, if properly managed and if proper trees are introduced, would, in the years ahead, be much more productive. This holds true in my part of the province where we had many fine stands of hardwood, but now these areas are cluttered up with tree tops and brush. They are of little value as pasture land and reforestation is the only hope of putting such properties back into useful production.
Since we have such large areas denuded by timber exploitation and erosion, our water levels have dropped so that many wells go

Marginal Lands Development dry for several months of the year. The minister through Bill No. C-77, hopes to rectify this situation, and I feel sure this can be accomplished with an accelerated reforestation program. I would suggest an immediate survey be made of the facilities available throughout the country for the production of seedlings. If more accommodation is required to supply the quantities needed, steps should be taken, in co-operation with the provincial governments, to get these establishments under way promptly. Reforestation, it seems to me, offers the best means to the end result which we hope will be accomplished by Bill No. C-77; that is, to state it briefly, to promote conservation in all elements and create better circumstances for rural people in the unsatisfactory income brackets. The benefits of reforestation would affect our whole economy. We have much secondary industry dependent on forest products. Wood has never been replaced as man's most valuable servant. Instead, thousands of new uses have been found for it and old uses have been continually improved.
Most of western Ontario is vitally concerned with the matter of water. Cities are exploiting the areas adjacent to them, and farm people in many localities are transporting water to their farms by tanks and milk cans. Reforestation, in the proper places, can do much to relieve this situation.
In our county of Grey, there is the highest point of land in Ontario, 1,735 feet above sea level. This is the great watershed of a vast territory of western Ontario. This great ridge, which embraces approximately 40,000 acres, should be completely reforested. In so doing, results would be forthcoming and, in a comparatively short time, the Grand, the Humber and the Credit rivers, which flow south, the Saugeen which flows west, and all the streams and rivers flowing north into Georgian Bay, could be restored to their natural flow, and with the assurance that spring floods would be at a minimum. The same program could be instituted at the head waters of all western Ontario rivers or in any other province where such conditions exist.
Without a doubt, the day is not far off when this program will be an absolute necessity, and I would commend it for early consideration, under this bill, with the co-operation of the provincial government.
These 40,000 acres of which I speak could also serve the purpose of a national park and game sanctuary. Under the authority of this bill more suitable areas should now be designated for national parks while choice virgin timbered locations are still available. Fire and exploitation have lost to our people some ideal territories for this purpose.

More game sanctuaries are required if we are to maintain our wildlife populations. We have thousands more joining the ranks of our hunters each year, and sport magazines continually report the scarcity of game in widespread areas. This is particularly true of the white-tail or red deer. Submarginal land or waste land could be converted to suitable game refuges.
Our local conservation authorities are to be commended for the contribution they have already made toward restoring our natural resources. Bill No. C-77 provides legislation that will extend the help and direction the authorities have hoped for, and of which they will not hesitate to take advantage.
This government should give some thought to introducing legislation in respect of the future settlement of all new areas in our country so that many of the obstacles we are now legislating to correct would be avoided.
Surrounded by a wealth of natural resources that seem inexhaustible, the pioneer in any area naturally shows more energy in using what is at hand to keep himself fed, warm, clothed and in business, than foresight in preserving any of it.
I am not in agreement with cutting our wheat acreage. This is a commodity that can be stored for lengthy periods. It is used for food the world over. It is not difficult to handle or transport. It could be our most potent weapon for maintaining peace. It could save millions of lives. It could save our own if great catastrophe overtook us. Our great western plains are reputed to be the bread basket of the world and, as such, they should continue. More of our wheat should go to those now starving. This will not hurt our market as these people are not in a position to buy. However, such humanitarian treatment could win them over politically now and for mutual economic advantage later.
I am in full accord with the remarks of President Kennedy when he said in his inauguration address "If a free society cannot help the many who are poor, it can never save the few who are rich".
In conclusion, 1 compliment the Minister of Agriculture on his initiative in respect to Bill No. C-77, the effects of which could permeate far into the future and affect many generations.
I would remind this house of what the scripture says through the prophet Isaiah:
"They that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places, Thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations, and thou shalt be called the repairer of the breach, the restorer of the paths to dwell in."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representing a riding where

there are many farmers, I consider it a privilege to comment tonight on this piece of legislation, one that is most important not only to the fanners in my area and farmers generally, but to everybody in Canada. (Text):
Mr. Speaker, at this stage in the debate three things have become most clear in the present legislation which is before us. First, it is legislation designed to keep Canadian farmers on the farms. Second, it is also designed to raise farm income in every section of this country, be it in the west or east. Third, it is legislation designed to give the farmers of this country a fair share of the national income. This is something that this government has striven for in the past, as it is striving for now.
In my brief remarks I would like to state that the legislation before us adheres to certain definite principles which this government always keeps before it in promoting legislation. In reading the present bill, hon. members will see that it is realized that the provinces and the local people know best what is best for themselves. Unlike other administrations, the present administration consults rather than dictates. Thus this is very broad legislation which sets out the purported agreements with the provinces on a local level. I repeat that this government believes most forcibly and truly in the principle that people know best what is best for themselves on the local level.
Another principle of this legislation relates to the notion that this government and this party have an obligation to the future. Up to the present time many speakers have outlined the fact that this legislation has to do with conservation and reforestation which will bear much fruit for farmers of future generations.
In past debates much was said about this pamphlet entitled, "A.R.D.A.," coming out in contravention of the rules of this house. There is nothing in this pamphlet which implicitly states that an act of parliament had already been passed. This pamphlet just goes to show that this government and this party do not dictate to the people what is good for them. We consult the people.
I can inform all hon. members that the farm forums right across this nation and all farm groups are taking a particular interest in this legislation. They are reading this pamphlet; they are discussing it in their farm forums in all parts of the country. I repeat, this pamphlet recognizes the fact that it is best first to consult with the people when legislation of this kind is put before parliament. I repeat, we consult, sir, we do not dictate.
Marginal Lands Development (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I wish also to congratulate and thank the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Jorgenson) for his remarks concerning the Mount Sutton development in the Brome-Missisquoi riding.
I can say that this project will be helpful not only to farmers in my area, but to the economy and to people in general.
I also wish to congratulate the Boulanger family, of Sutton, and their associates for their noteworthy initiative. This is a good example for many regions of our young country, Canada.
(Text):
I should just like to mention, sir, the initiative that is being shown by the citizens of Sutton regarding the development so ably mentioned by the hon. member for Proven-cher (Mr. Jorgenson) the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture. With him, I should like to congratulate the citizens of Sutton on the initiative they have shown in the Mount Sutton development. So far as this bill is concerned, it shows what can be done when action and enterprise of this sort are undertaken. The present legislation is being discussed by farmers and farm forums throughout the length and breadth of this land.
In his remarks yesterday the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate tried to suggest that possibly while the government did not intend this to happen, farmers earning a gross or a net income of $1,200 a year or less would be forced to leave the farm. Such is not the case. The real intent behind this legislation is to raise farm income and to keep farmers on the farms. I think it would be irresponsible to suggest that either directly or indirectly this is legislation which will encourage farmers to leave the farms. It is most irresponsible to suggest, as was done indirectly by certain hon. members, that this legislation will drive farmers in the low income brackets off their farms. I know this was suggested in my own area by certain individuals and I should like to deny this rumour right here and now. As I said at the outset of my remarks, this is legislation designed to keep farmers on the farm, to raise farm incomes and to give the farmers of this nation a fair share of the national income.
I am sure it is legislation which will be received well not only by farmers in my area but by the farmers in all sections and in all provinces of this country. For that reason, along with other hon. members who have just spoken, I should like to commend it to hon. members.
